articles.title: Could this be the year Democrats close the 'governor gap' with Republicans?
articles.summary: Republican governors have outnumbered Democratic governors for more than a decade. Key contests in red states like Iowa and Texas could change that.
articles.body:
When people talk about this year's midterms, they tend to focus on whether Democrats will end unified Republican control of Congress by winning the U.S. Senate or House of Representatives (or both). And that makes sense: Congress has the power to check President Trump's agenda, so the national repercussions could be huge.

But on Election Day, there will be something else to watch out for: whether Democrats can emerge with more governors' mansions than Republicans.

GOP governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). That's given Republicans more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and build executive experience.

But this year, Democrats have a real shot at closing the "governor gap." They need to net one governorship to tie Republicans at 25; net two, and they'll secure a gubernatorial "majority" for the first time since 2011. At the moment, 16 of this year's 36 gubernatorial contests are considered competitive, according to the expert race handicappers at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report — and 11 of them are in Republican-held states.

So Democrats are on offense. It remains to be seen, however, whether they will actually overcome decades of GOP gubernatorial dominance in places like Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas on Nov. 3. Here are the races to watch.

Alaska hasn't elected a Democratic governor in 28 years. But that could change on Nov. 3 as Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins — known locally as JKT — has emerged as the frontrunner to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. In part, that's due to the Last Frontier's unique voting system, which sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference, from first to fourth. As a result, Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former state representative, is the only Democrat competing against three Republicans: conservative activist Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor.

But economic dissatisfaction, Trump's low approval ratings in the state and Kreiss-Tomkins's energetic campaign are also helping to boost Democratic hopes. Recent polls suggest Kreiss-Tomkins could win the first round of ranked-choice balloting with nearly 50% of the vote — roughly twice as much as the second-place candidate (Wilson). On Oct. 13, Cook shifted its race rating from "toss up" to "lean Democrat." Along with Iowa, the outlet wrote, Alaska "may be Democrats' best opportunity to flip a governors' mansion in a red state."

A former swing state, Florida has trended increasingly Republican during the Trump era. The governor's mansion, however, has been red ever since Jeb Bush won the job in 1998. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds — the third Black Republican in history to represent the Sunshine State on Capitol Hill — is seeking to keep the GOP's streak alive by succeeding term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. His opponent is Democrat David Jolly , a former Republican congressman who left the GOP during Trump's first term.

The president endorsed Donalds, a staunch social conservative, before he even entered the race; in Congress, Donalds has closely aligned himself with Trump's MAGA policies , especially on immigration. Meanwhile, Jolly is emphasizing his Christian faith, his conversion from Republican to independent to Democrat and his approach to key local issues like homeowner's insurance (which involves creating a state-backed catastrophe fund to keep costs down).

Recent polls mostly show Donalds — who has raised more than seven times as much money as Jolly — leading by single-digit margins, with less than 50% of the vote; a few suggest a tie. Cook rates the race as "lean Republican."

Georgia has become the purplest of purple states in recent years: Trump lost it by 0.2 percentage points in 2020 and won it by 2 points in 2024. But while Georgians have sent two Democrats to the U.S. Senate in recent years — Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff — they haven't elected a Democratic governor since 1998.

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has a chance to break the pattern on Nov. 3. The polls show her within striking distance — anywhere from 1 to 3 percentage points — of health care billionaire Rick Jackson, who won the GOP nomination without Trump's endorsement. Both candidates are promising to lower the cost of living by lowering taxes — a mainstream message in a relatively centrist state. Jackson has a huge financial edge , but Cook still rates the race as a toss up.

If elected, Bottoms would make history as Georgia's first woman governor and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the U.S.

Iowa is another state that hasn't elected a Democratic governor in decades — 20 years to be exact. But state auditor Rob Sand, 44, has led in every poll conducted this cycle , often by double-digit margins.

As auditor — and before that, as Iowa's assistant attorney general — Sand developed a reputation as a "happy warrior for nonpartisan technocratic efficiency and anti-corruption," a leading progressive activist recently told the Atlantic . He has also downplayed his allegiance to the national Democratic Party, calling it "the lesser of two evils." Such positioning has made Sand perhaps the most popular politician in a state where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by almost 200,000.

Sand's opponent, businessman Zach Lahn, narrowly upset Trump's pick, Rep. Randy Feenstra, in this summer's Republican primary. A Kansas resident until 2023, Lahn has struggled to overcome accusations of carpetbagging ever since. Cook says the race "leans Democrat" and describes it as the party's best pickup opportunity.

Kansas is anything but a blue state; since 1940, it has voted Republican in every presidential election but one — Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide. But the Sunflower State has elected two Democratic women governors in recent years: Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027). State Sen. Cindy Holscher is seeking to become the third.

Holscher has her work cut out for her, though. She's up against Ty Masterson, the president of the state Senate, who leads by a few percentage points in most recent polls . Cook rates the Kansas contest as "lean Republican," making it this year's only potential blue-to-red flip with that rating.

If Masterson does win in November, it wouldn't be particularly surprising. Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's mansion for longer than eight consecutive years.

Incumbent GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo — the former sheriff of Clark County — won in 2022 on a law-and-order message. But Nevada is a swing state, and Lombardo's insistence on vetoing a raft of affordability bills passed by the Democratic legislature — to cap the cost of prescription drugs; to provide paid family leave to workers; to prohibit private equity and big banks from buying up housing en masse; to continue universal free breakfast and lunch for K-12 schoolchildren — has become a source of criticism in a cycle often centered on the cost of living. And his previous support for data-center subsidies hasn't helped .

Enter state Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running on his working-class roots . Only two polls have been conducted since Labor Day. One shows Ford ahead by 2 points; the other shows Lombardo leading by 2. Cook rates the race a "toss up."

On paper, the odds are against Amy Acton, a Democrat who previously served as Ohio's chief public health officer . In 2024, Trump won the Buckeye State by the widest presidential margin since Ronald Reagan — more than 11 percentage points — and Democrats have lost all but one gubernatorial contest there since 1990.

But most recent polls have shown Acton leading billionaire pharmaceutical and biotech entrepreneur (and former GOP presidential candidate) Vivek Ramaswamy — often by a decent margin. And while the race has been one of the "ugliest in the country," according to a recent New York Times report — "with exaggerated portrayals of one candidate as a con artist and the other as a drunk" — voters there continue to hold a narrowly favorable view of Acton and a narrowly unfavorable view of Ramaswamy .

Greg Abbott has been governor of Texas since 2015. Before that, he was Texas attorney general for more than a dozen years. He's perhaps the most familiar Republican politician in a state where Republicans have long dominated politics.

But even Abbott is at risk this cycle. Beyond the overall environment — which favors Democrats — the governor has faced backlash over Flock cameras, school privatization, data centers and his close ties to Trump. (Abbott skipped the president's campaign stop in San Antonio last week, saying he had a scheduling conflict.) He's also facing a strong challenger in Gina Hinojosa, who has pitched herself as more "populist" than "progressive ."

The latest polls show Abbott and Hinojosa trading small leads ahead of Election Day. Cook says the race "leans Republican."

After Gov. Tony Evers declined to seek a third term, democratic socialist Francesca Hong emerged as the frontrunner to win Wisconsin's Democratic primary in August. Milwaukee County executive David Crowley dropped out in mid-July — then re-entered the race 10 days later. With Evers's endorsement, he was able to edge Hong for the nod.

The idea behind Crowley's last-minute comeback was that he would be more electable than Hong, who raised eyebrows with her past statements calling for the U.S. to "cancel" Thanksgiving and "abolish" the police. Recent polling has been consistent with that theory, showing Crowley consistently leading U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany — but only by single-digit margins. Cook rates the race a "toss up."

If elected, Crowley would be Wisconsin's first Black governor.

According to Cook, there are three states where Democrats currently hold the governorship that could be considered competitive: Arizona (Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vs. Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs); Oregon (Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek vs. Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan); and Michigan (Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson vs. Republican U.S. Rep. John James). Cook rates all three as "lean Democratic."

Cook also recently moved three states from "solid Republican" to "likely Republican," reflecting movement toward the Democratic candidate. They are Nebraska (Republican Gov. Jim Pillen vs. Democratic former state Sen. Lynne Walz); Oklahoma (Republican former state Sen. Mike Mazzei vs. Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson); and Vermont (Republican Gov. Phil Scott vs. Democratic economist Amanda Janoo).

A fourth Republican-held state, New Hampshire, is also in the "likely Republican" category. GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte is facing Democratic former executive councilor Cinde Warmington.

articles.title: The 2026 midterms polls are predicting a blue wave. Can they be trusted?
articles.summary: After major misses in recent elections, some experts say there's reason to look at polls predicting a Democratic landslide with a healthy dose of skepticism.
articles.body:
Anyone who's followed American politics over the past decade or so has learned to look at political polls with a healthy dose of skepticism. Some of the most important recent elections have featured substantial polling errors that left many Americans baffled when things turned out differently than they expected.

As we head into a pivotal midterm election, the polls are generally telling the same story. Forecasts point to the possibility of a blue wave that will sweep across the country, likely allowing Democrats to flip control of the House of Representatives and giving them a chance of gaining a majority in the Senate as well.

Is that story true, though? We won't know for certain until after the actual votes are counted, but there is evidence that can give us a slightly better sense of what the polls are seeing, what they might be missing and how well other political trends match the picture that the polls are painting.

In a midterm election, there are three types of polls to watch if you want a sense of where things stand in the battle for control of Congress.

The first tracks the approval rating of someone who isn't even on the ballot in November: the president of the United States. Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Knowing how Americans feel about the president's job performance is helpful because they tend to channel those feelings into their votes for the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. Right now, 60% of Americans, on average, disapprove of how President Trump is handling his job, according to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin ; 38% approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at about 22 percentage points.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 46-point gap.

The second type of poll to pay attention to is what's known (at least among politics nerds) as the "generic ballot," which typically asks something along the lines of: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? This is our best measure of how partisan sentiment is shaping up across all 435 U.S. House contests. At the moment, Democrats have a lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average — and Republican support has been trending downward since September.

To put that in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. Three weeks later, Democrats picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. (This year, Democrats need to net only three seats to win control of that chamber.)

The third and final type of polling that matters in a congressional midterm cycle is state surveys of key Senate contests. Here's where the data gets a little trickier. In recent weeks, the preponderance of polling has shown Democrats widening their leads in competitive states where they're defending seats they already hold ( Georgia , Minnesota , New Hampshire , Michigan ) while also gaining ground in red states where they're trying to flip a Republican-held seat ( Alaska , Iowa , Texas , Kansas , Ohio ).

Some Republicans are arguing that this red-state Senate polling could be inaccurate — and pointing to past polling "misses" to make their case.

How badly have polls missed in the past?

It's important to note that polling errors should be expected in any race. Polling is an inexact science. No matter how sophisticated a pollster's process is, it invariably includes assumptions, adjustments and extrapolations that leave a lot of room for error. That uncertainty has been a feature of election polling throughout its history.

Those misses are less impactful in years where the variance in polls balances out. If they underestimate the Republicans' strength in some races while overselling the GOP in others, you end up with polling that generally reflects the actual results in the aggregate.

The problem over the past decade is that, in multiple elections, the polls have mostly missed in the same direction.

Trump's win over Hillary Clinton in 2016 came as such a surprise because polls had systematically underestimated his support. When it came to the national popular vote , the polls were relatively accurate. The big misses came in the swing states that decided the election. Heading into Election Day, polls showed Clinton ahead — sometimes by a large margin — in five states that Trump ended up winning. The 2016 election sparked a reckoning within the polling world. The major polling firms realized that something had made them underestimate the size of Trump's voting coalition. They spent years making changes to how they collect and interpret data to fix that clear blind spot.

Things looked more promising after the 2018 midterms. The polls were reasonably accurate. When they did miss, they missed in both directions, meaning the polls weren't systematically biased against either party.

Then came 2020. Even though the polls accurately predicted Joe Biden would win, they underestimated Republicans' support by even more than they had four years earlier. Trump performed nearly 3 percentage points better than expected in the national popular vote and outperformed polls in individual states by more than 4 points. The miss was even bigger in Senate and gubernatorial races.

The polls bounced back in 2022, when they were more accurate than in any election in recent history, before once again underestimating Republicans in 2024 — though by a smaller margin than in either 2016 or 2020.

The pattern over the past decade has been that polls have tended to be biased against Republicans when Trump is on the ballot and reasonably on point when he's not. While that could be considered reason for optimism among Democrats, five election cycles is hardly a definitive sample.

A lot of explanations have been put forward to try to understand the polling misses in recent presidential elections. The most commonly cited is the belief that MAGA Republicans, due to their general lack of trust in mainstream institutions, are less likely to pick up the phone when a polling firm calls than members of other political groups. That phenomenon, which pollsters call "nonresponse bias," can skew survey samples and make the share of Republican voters appear smaller than it really is.

"The polling is wrong. ... Republicans don't want to respond to polls anymore," House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Tuesday.

Johnson and other Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side to bolster their argument that polls might be missing GOP voters. That includes Democratic leads and strong showings by independents in Senate races in deep red states like Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska . For those polls to be accurate, voter sentiment would have had to have swung as much as 23 points in Democrats' direction since the last midterm Senate contests in those states.

One pollster recently described GOP voters' nonresponse in a poll they conducted in Iowa as a "canary in the cornfields" for a potentially widespread undercounting of Republican support in the state.

Polling firms try to account for nonresponse bias by adjusting their results to give less weight to people from groups who are overrepresented in their samples, but doing so means making a lot of assumptions about the nature of a constantly evolving electorate. It's possible that the adjustments they're making this year aren't enough to accurately reflect voters' sentiments.

On top of gauging how people will vote, there's also the challenge of determining who will vote. Polls often include results for "likely" voters — voters who are expected to cast a ballot — but deciding who should fit into that category involves its own assumptions that can be wrong. Earlier this month, the polling firm YouGov released a survey showing Democrats up 16 points nationally with likely voters, a gap that YouGov itself described as "hard-to-believe."

While the major recent polling errors have been in presidential election years, data compiled by Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini suggests that the polls have also had some noteworthy misses in midterm cycles as well.

"Nationally, the polls were pretty good, but red state polls were too blue and blue state polls too red," he wrote on X .

If Ruffini's analysis is accurate, that could mean that Democrats' chances of flipping Senate seats in states like Texas, Iowa and Ohio aren't nearly as strong as they appear to be.

Republicans also have more room for error in the House this year thanks to redistricting. The GOP's sweeping campaign to redraw congressional maps in red states gave them up to nine new safe House seats. Democrats tried to even the score by doing their own gerrymandering. But when the dust settled, Republicans still came out ahead.

That said, Republicans might still struggle to keep their majority in the House even if the polls are off by a significant margin. On the other hand, when it comes to the Senate, the polls would only need to be off by a few points in a handful of key states for the GOP to maintain control over the chamber.

Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another .

The argument that skeptics are making this time around is that there is something fundamentally different about the Trump era — something that systematically skews all poll results involving Trump.

This has been true, to a degree, in each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in. There, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver .

But there has been no systematic polling bias toward Democrats in Trump-era elections when Trump himself was not on the ballot . In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver .

One possible explanation for this dynamic is that "the midterm electorate skews toward politically engaged voters who are more trusting of institutions and more likely to have answered polls," as the Atlantic recently put it . To be significantly wrong in 2026, the polls would have to be wrong in ways they weren't in 2022 and 2018.

There are other reasons to believe the polls could be right as well. While there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states , that doesn't necessarily mean that those voters are secretly planning to show up and surprise everyone on Election Day. Instead, experts say that it might mean the opposite: that they don't want to answer questions about politics because they are not particularly enthusiastic about voting this year. Pollsters aren't seeing this "rural nonresponse" effect everywhere , either.

The parties are also behaving as if the polls are accurate. Republicans' spending patterns show that they are "pour[ing] money into dozens of U.S. House races previously considered 'safe,'" Reuters recently reported . Democrats are also campaigning hard in parts of the country that would typically be out of their reach.

Meanwhile, "some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections," according to Politico .

On the Senate side, the major GOP campaign groups have reportedly cut back on spending in North Carolina and Georgia, a sign that they may be losing faith in winning those races, and rerouted the money to defend a historically safe seat in Kansas.

None of this guarantees that the polls are right. They could be rife with the same errors that have plagued them in recent elections, or have new blind spots that won't become clear until later. However, the polls currently reflect what you might expect to see in a political environment in which historical precedent suggests the party in power will struggle, the president's approval rating is low, and the parties are battling it out in what are normally deep red parts of the country.

We'll find out just how accurate the polls really are on Nov. 3.

articles.title: Voter ID rules are in the spotlight ahead of the midterms. Here's what you need to know before heading to the polls.
articles.summary: A Supreme Court order on New Hampshire's voter ID law has put identification requirements back in focus.
articles.body:
The Supreme Court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to enforce a ban on voters using student ID as proof of identity at the polls in November's midterm elections .

In its decision Thursday, the court paused a federal court's ruling that would have allowed poll workers to consider student IDs to verify voters' identities without an approved government-issued ID. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only Supreme Court justice to dissent publicly.

The court action came after New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene after telling election officials that he wouldn't accept student IDs even as backup identification in this year's midterms. Earlier this year, a Republican-backed law removed student ID from the list of identification voters can use to get a ballot.

The Coalition for Open Democracy, which is challenging the ban, wrote in a statement on Instagram that the decision was "wrong" and upheld "an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote."

Republican New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella praised the ruling. "New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written," he said in a statement . "The Supreme Court's decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials."

The decision comes amid a broader push for tighter election rules, including limiting the ID voters can use to verify their identity at the ballot box. The Trump administration is pursuing stricter citizenship verification and voter-registration enforcement ahead of Nov. 3.

In Ohio, voters will also decide on Nov. 3 whether to add the state's existing photo ID requirement to its constitution, making it harder for future lawmakers to change or repeal.

With voter ID requirements under scrutiny across the country , here's what voters need to know about which forms of identification are accepted at the polls — and what happens if they don't have one.

Voter ID requirements vary across the U.S., with some states requiring photo identification at the polls and others accepting documents without a photograph.

According to the National Conference of State Legislatures , 36 states have laws requiring or requesting some form of identification when voting in person. The remaining 14 states and Washington, D.C., use other methods to verify voters' identities, such as checking signatures or personal information. These states are: California, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Vermont.

In states requiring photo ID, accepted documents may include a driver's license, state-issued identification card or U.S. passport. Other states allow documents without photos, such as utility bills or bank statements.

The rules on student IDs vary by state. While New Hampshire has restricted their use, some states, including North Carolina, accept student IDs that meet specific requirements.

Voters can check the rules for their state through Vote.gov or their local election office before heading to the polls.

What happens if you show up to cast your vote without an approved ID?

Voters who arrive at the polls without an approved form of identification may still be able to cast a ballot, depending on their state's rules.

Some states allow voters to verify their identity through alternative methods, such as signing an affidavit, while others offer provisional ballots, which allow someone to vote while election officials check their eligibility and whether their ballot can be counted.

However, in some states, voters must provide the right identification or complete additional verification steps within a set deadline after Election Day for their provisional ballot to count.

The National Conference of State Legislatures outlines these different procedures, while voters can check their state's specific requirements through Vote.gov or their local election office.

For those voting by mail, identification and verification requirements also vary by state. The Trump administration sought to introduce new nationwide restrictions on the mailing of ballots, but the Supreme Court blocked the changes from taking effect before this year's midterms.

Voters planning to cast an absentee or mail-in ballot should check their state's requirements and deadlines through Vote.gov.

Where does the Trump administration stand on voter ID?

President Trump has made tightening election security a priority for his administration, pushing for stricter citizenship checks and changes to how voter eligibility is verified.

"There will be Voter I.D. for the Midterm Elections, whether approved by Congress or not!" the president wrote on Truth Social in February. "Also, the People of our Country are insisting on Citizenship, and No Mail-In Ballots, with exceptions for Military, Disability, Illness, or Travel."

In March, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to compile lists of confirmed U.S. citizens to help states verify voter eligibility. An earlier executive order sought to require documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections, but a federal judge blocked that requirement.

Some groups have criticized broader efforts to tighten voter ID and citizenship rules. The Brennan Center for Justice estimates that more than 21 million Americans of voting age lack ready access to proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate.

articles.title: Have you been checked out of politics? This 2026 midterms guide is for you.
articles.summary: Everything you need to know to get caught up before Election Day, all in one place.
articles.body:
Politics can be a lot. Keeping track of what's going on can be confusing, frustrating, unsettling and, often, pretty boring. It's no surprise that a large share of Americans feel compelled to step back from following politics or give up on it entirely.

As understandable as it is to give yourself some distance, that does mean it can be hard to get caught up when something important — like next week's big midterm election — comes up. That's exactly what this story is meant to help with.

There's no need to bombard you with every single twist and turn in U.S. politics since President Trump was elected to a second term two years ago. Instead, consider this a zoomed-out, stripped-down cheat sheet of the things you really do need to know to understand what's happening, why it matters and how you can take part yourself on Nov. 3.

The midterms happen in even years when there's not a presidential election (they're called that because they happen in the middle of a president's term).

This year, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, as well as 35 of 100 Senate seats and the governorship of 36 states, are on the ballot. That means every eligible voter in all 50 states has the chance to, at minimum, vote for their congressional representative. Voters in 26 states can cast their ballots for all three.

Presidential races are obviously the headliner when it comes to U.S. elections, but midterms are very important too. Republicans have had a "trifecta" — control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency — since January 2025. Unified control in Washington has allowed Republicans to turn Trump's favored legislation — like his One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a tax and spending plan — into law. It has also helped Trump get allies like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. confirmed to his Cabinet and made it harder for Democrats to rein in Trump's military actions in Iran..

Flipping just one chamber of Congress would give Democrats an effective veto on any legislation Republicans wanted to pass over the final two years of Trump's presidency. It would also provide them with leverage during negotiations over must-pass legislation, like government funding bills or the defense budget. House Democrats are already signaling plans to launch a wide range of investigations into the president and his allies , and even potentially pursue impeachment proceedings , if they gain control of the chamber.

Taking over both the House and Senate would give Democrats even more power to block Trump's agenda. With both chambers under their control, they could pass their own legislation, potentially forcing the president to veto popular bills. They would also have the ability to block Trump's nominees for Cabinet positions from being confirmed and prevent him from filling any vacancies that arise on the Supreme Court.

The midterms will also have a major impact on individual states, including a number of key swing states where the governorship is up for grabs.

For months, polls have generally suggested that we could see a "blue wave" of Democratic victories across the country. But whether that happens, and how big the wave might be, remains to be seen.

Forecasters generally expect Democrats to take back the House, potentially with a significant majority. There's much more uncertainty about the Senate. Right now, the polls are showing Democrats doing much better than they historically have in some of the traditionally Republican states, like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. At the same time, races in some swing states also appear to be quite close. That means that any of the dozen or so competitive Senate contests could be the one that decides control of the chamber.

The polls could be wrong, of course. They have underestimated Republicans to varying degrees in three separate elections during the Trump era. Even a polling error of a few percentage points could mean Republicans wouldn't have to worry about losing the Senate, though the House could still flip. Those recent polling errors were all presidential years, however. The polls have been more accurate over the past two midterm cycles.

Midterms also tend to go poorly for the party that controls the presidency, especially when the president's approval rating is low — as Trump's is right now.

Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but he looms large over the most important issues of the midterms: cost of living and the economy, which are at least partially tied to the president's tariffs and the war in Iran. A recent survey found that both were at the top of the list when voters were asked which issues will influence their votes the most.

Candidates from both parties have focused heavily on affordability in their midterm messages, with Democrats blaming Trump and the GOP for rising costs, and some Republicans breaking from the president by calling for an end to the war or the reversal of tariffs .

A recent poll showed that most voters want Congress to exert more influence over Trump's policies, either to roll them back or to act as a check on his actions.

Other polls have shown that voters are highly concerned about corruption in government and protecting America's democracy. Issues like health care, immigration, education and crime are also weighing heavily on voters, as they do in most elections.

Many Republicans have made the issue of transgender rights, specifically trans athletes' participation in girls' and women's sports, a significant part of their midterm message. Though polls show that Americans share concerns about trans athletes playing in these sports, other surveys suggest the issue ranks low on the list of factors that will influence how they vote.

One topic that's emerged as a major election issue for many voters this year is data centers. These facilities, which house the servers and other infrastructure that allow the internet to function, have become a point of contention for voters who oppose having them built in their communities. The American public's opposition to data center construction has grown remarkably quickly, and candidates from both parties are adjusting their positions on the fly to try to keep up with voters' opinions.

About 80% of the 435 total House races on the ballot are not considered to be competitive. That leaves about 80 or so districts that could decide which party wins control of the House. The majority of those competitive seats are currently held by Republicans, which means they face a steep challenge as they try to hold on to their narrow House majority. In fact, many forecasters believe Democrats will take over the chamber.

"Republicans' path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated," Erin Covey, an analyst with the nonpartisan Cook Political Report , wrote last week.

The real question about the House seems to be: If Democrats win control of the chamber, how many seats will they win?

The fate of the Senate is much less certain. Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to secure a majority. To do that, they'll have to defend the vulnerable seats they currently hold in swing states while also flipping at least a couple seats in typically Republican states.

Polls suggest that control of the Senate could hinge on whether Republicans can hold their ground in conservative states like Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas. It's also worth paying attention to Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, where the GOP could make up for any losses in Republican-leaning states by flipping Democrat-held seats.

The list of competitive gubernatorial races looks a lot like the list of competitive Senate races. Democrats are on defense in swing states like Wisconsin, Minnesota and Arizona while also eyeing upsets in red states. The Cook Political Report gives Democrats a slight advantage in three states that currently have Republican governors (Ohio, Alaska and Iowa) and list two others (Nevada and Georgia) as toss-ups.

Just two Democratic-led states (Wisconsin and Kansas) are considered either toss-ups or leaning Republican.

There is a long list of major ballot measures that will be decided on Election Day. That includes two significant abortion-related initiatives. Idaho will vote on whether to override its strict abortion laws and establish a right to abortion until fetal viability, while Missouri will decide whether to roll back abortion protections that were approved by voters just two years ago.

Four states (Washington, Nebraska, Arizona and Colorado) will consider initiatives that would bar transgender athletes from participating in girls' and women's sports. Three states (California, Colorado and Nevada) will decide whether to establish or expand laws requiring voters to show ID when they cast their ballots. Voters in five states (California, Utah, North Dakota, South Dakota and Idaho) are considering proposals that would make it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law.

There are also some significant races happening at the local level. Twenty-two of the 100 biggest cities in the U.S. will choose their mayors on Election Day. That includes Los Angeles, where moderate Democrat Karen Bass is facing a tough challenge from progressive City Council Member Nithya Raman — who some commentators are calling L.A.'s equivalent to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Maybe not. It depends on your registration status and where you live. The first step is to find out if you're already registered to vote. You can do that here . If you are currently registered, it may still be possible to vote early or request a mail ballot in your state. You can find out the specific deadlines for your state here or by checking your state government's voter information website. Info on early voting can be found here

Even if you're not registered, you may still have a chance to vote. Twenty-one states and Washington, D.C. allow same-day voter registration on Election Day.

articles.title: Democratic women could make history in midterm governor and House races
articles.summary: They're chasing a record number of governorships and 100 House seats.
articles.body:
Four years ago, eight Democratic women won governorships in a single election, a milestone that reshaped the map.

This November, Democrats aim to elect even more -- including in red states -- and to push the number of Democratic women in the U.S. House past 100. Candidates and organizations on the left told ABC News both milestones are plausible, but they rest on winning the most competitive races.

Twenty-six women are major-party nominees overall, one more than the 2022 record of 25. There are 19 Democratic women gubernatorial nominees, a record that's up from 16 in 2022. Republicans have seven women nominees in governor's races, down from nine in 2022.

Kelly Dittmar of Rutgers' Center for American Women and Politics said Democrats have "a more robust support infrastructure" than Republicans specifically targeting women in politics, including trainings, recruitment programs, PACs and funding, which she says strengthens the pipeline to elected office.

Sarah Chamberlain, a GOP strategist and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, argues that "finding Republican women who want to run" is the challenge rather the party's support infrastructure.

"The numbers are not as high as the Democratic women, and they've really never been, but absolutely, there is an entire Republican Party … open to welcoming women, and it's just that the candidates this year tended to be more men," Chamberlain said.

In Ohio, Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy has faced bipartisan backlash for his attack ad against Democratic nominee Amy Acton. The ad features Acton's estranged mother, whom Acton says stood by the man criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child before his death in 2004.

Acton would be Ohio's first woman governor and has railed against Ramaswamy for doubling down on the ad in recent speeches, including at her rally alongside former President Barack Obama.

She told ABC News : "I'm a scrappy kid from Youngstown. I've seen a thing or two, and I'm up for this fight. But kindness shouldn't be seen as weakness."

Michigan Democrat Jocelyn Benson said in an interview that her miscarriage has shaped her healthcare message when speaking to voters. She noted that federal funding cuts have closed three Planned Parenthood clinics in the state, including the only one in the Upper Peninsula.

"Behind every clinic closure is a woman who has to drive two extra hours for care or go without it," Benson said.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, the state's first Democratic woman governor, said party strategists drew the wrong lesson after 2024. Too many insiders concluded that Democrats needed to be crass and create a "male bro culture" to look tough, she said, but that approach has been unsuccessful while "steely-eyed women" have been successful. Voters, she says, value authenticity.

Several nominees could break barriers. Gina Hinojosa would be the first Latina governor of Texas. In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland would be the first Native American woman to serve as a governor. Keisha Lance Bottoms would be Georgia's first woman governor and the first Black woman to govern any state.

"We didn't believe as a country that the nation would elect a Black president ... and it happened. So it's possible, it just hasn't happened yet. And for me, it's much more personal ... We can trace our family to a plantation in Crawfordville, Georgia," Bottoms told ABC's Linsey Davis .

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey chairs the Democratic Governors Association's Women Governors Fund. Since 2018, the DGA has invested over $120 million to elect and re-elect the current class of Democratic women governors.

The DGA has put $1 million into Texas, but the group and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, have faced pressure from some prominent Latino Democrats to invest $10 million in Hinojosa's race.

Appearing with Bottoms at a rally in Georgia on Monday, Beshear announced the DGA was investing $5 million more into her race, which followed an announcement earlier this month of a $10 million investment in Bottoms' race against billionaire businessman Rick Jackson.

Healey told ABC News, "Gina is a great candidate, and I believe she can win. And it is to her credit that she has made this a winnable race."

The push for 100 Democratic women in the House

Ninety-five Democratic women currently serve as voting members in the House, and 198 Democratic women are on the general election ballot. Elect Democratic Women, a political action committee that supports Democratic women candidates, hope to elect at least 100 women to the House -- which would be the most ever.

As for Republican women, there are 30 voting members currently serving in the House, down from 34 in the 118th Congress. There are 73 GOP women on the general election ballot. Dittmar maintains that a new record for Republican women is unlikely, and a drop from current levels is possible given the political headwinds facing Republicans this year.

Chamberlain acknowledged Republicans' uphill climb, saying, "If the polling is right, some [Republican] women and a whole lot of men are going to lose their seats."

Rep. Lois Frankel, who chairs Elect Democratic Women, said it supports women candidates both emotionally and financially. She argued that women's presence in government matters.

"Women were excluded from medical research until Pat Schroeder and Nancy Pelosi got on Appropriations [Committee] and fought for them," Frankel said.

Denise Powell, the Democratic candidate in Nebraska's 2nd District, would be the first woman to hold the seat. She said the group's support carried her through a six-way primary.

Powell, whose children are 16 and 12, talks often on the trail about motherhood. She argues too few mothers of young kids serve in Congress, "and I think that explains why there are so many policies that do nothing to support working parents."

articles.title: Who is Abdul El-Sayed? A guide to the Michigan Democrat in one of the midterms' biggest Senate races
articles.summary: His progressive policies, confrontational approach and Muslim faith have made him a target of persistent Republican attacks. Can he still win in one of Ameri...
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in Michigan's critical Senate race, responded to President Trump's frequent mockery of his name in a style that's become a signature of his campaign.

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," he said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Sunday. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

El-Sayed, whose middle name is Mohamed, has emerged as one of the biggest names of the 2026 midterm cycle as he tries to defend a vulnerable Senate seat in one of the country's few truly purple states. Michigan is key to Democrats' hopes of flipping control of the Senate, which requires them to defend their vulnerable seats and secure wins in several historically red states.

On paper, El-Sayed doesn't fit the profile of a "safe" choice for a swing state Democratic candidate. He's an unapologetic progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel. He's willing to be confrontational with his critics and publicly critique his party's establishment. He's vying to be the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate.

El-Sayed became the Democratic nominee in August, after narrowly defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, a relative moderate, in one of the most closely watched party primaries of the midterm cycle. His Republican opponent in the general election is Mike Rogers, a former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago.

Here's everything you need to know about one of the key figures of the 2026 midterms.

El-Sayed, 41, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science.

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his M.D. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department.

In 2018, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 points. "It was just like, 'Everything's moving really fast. I don't know what to pay attention to,'" El-Sayed recently recalled , likening his rookie bid to playing up an age level in lacrosse for the first time.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. At first, the Democratic primary pitted El-Sayed and Stevens against Michigan State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, and polls showed the three candidates splitting the vote fairly evenly. But after El-Sayed started to gain momentum over the spring and summer, McMorrow announced in early July that she was suspending her campaign.

In the lead-up to primary day, polls showed El-Sayed with a sizable lead in his head-to-head matchup against Stevens. The race was much closer than expected. He ended up winning by a single percentage point.

El-Sayed has made headlines for his outspoken criticism of Israel; the leading pro-Israel lobbying group, AIPAC; and U.S. political candidates who accept AIPAC money.

While El-Sayed has insisted that " the question of Israel's existence is not a question ," he has also said he doesn't " believe in ethno-states ." He has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump."

"Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April . "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both."

El-Sayed has also called for ending all unconditional U.S. aid to Israel. His argument is that "we should be using our tax dollars here to invest in health care here and education here, rather than sending it over there to buy bombs and tanks that get used to drive apartheid and genocide." During the primary, he frequently dismissed Stevens — who does not believe there has been a genocide in Gaza and who has received a record $30 million from AIPAC — as " a suit with a large AIPAC bank account ."

Beyond Israel and Gaza, El-Sayed has aligned himself with the Sanders wing of the Democratic Party. He has endorsed Medicare for All, promised to end Citizens United, backed targeted tariffs and bemoaned corporate monopolies. El-Sayed also wants to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and replace it with something like the former Immigration and Naturalization Service.

El-Sayed does not identify as a democratic socialist, even though many of his supporters do. The Democratic Socialists of America have not endorsed him.

Some of the buzz surrounding El-Sayed is just straightforward controversy; he has campaigned , for instance, with Hasan Piker, a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American .

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies.

Democratic anxiety is also a factor. El-Sayed has clearly benefited from rising anger on the left toward Israel; nearly 60% of Democrats now believe their party is too supportive of the Jewish state, according to a June AP-NORC survey — a 15-point increase over the last two years.

But some Democrats also worry about alienating the broader electorate, especially in a swing state like Michigan. As a result, El-Sayed's primary battle against Stevens morphed into a proxy war between "progressives pushing the party to rethink its relationship with Israel," as the New York Times recently put it , and "establishment Democrats feeling queasy about El-Sayed's electability" — as well as "some Jews fearing where he could take the party."

The biggest reason El-Sayed is attracting so much national attention, however, is the same reason he won the Democratic primary: charisma. After El-Sayed delivered the student speech at his 2007 Michigan commencement ceremony, the other speaker, former President Bill Clinton, told him he had "a natural gift."

"Dear Abdul," Clinton wrote to El-Sayed three days later. "Your commencement speech was terrific — I wish you well and will try to live long enough to need you as my doctor."

In general, El-Sayed has been less focused on Israel than on economic populism. To gin up enthusiasm among disaffected progressives, El-Sayed directs some of that "fighter" energy at the Democratic establishment. But most of it he directs upward, at the corporate elite.

"So when they tell us that we cannot have health care?" he asks his supporters at the end of his speeches.

"When they tell us that their money is unbeatable?"

"When they tell us we can't have a union in our workplace?"

El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans. Beyond mocking his name, Trump has called him a "jihadist" and accused him of being "on the side of the terrorists." Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. Rogers has falsely claimed that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion of the question: The assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith.

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After initially trailing, El-Sayed overtook Rogers in the polls in mid-August and has maintained a steady lead of 3-4 points on average in the months leading up to Election Day. Still, the race is considered a toss-up by the Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters.

articles.title: Daylight saving time has ended. Here's when clocks spring forward
articles.summary: The end of daylight saving time means more sleep but less daylight. Here is when clocks will spring forward next year.
articles.body:
Most people in the United States can expect clocks to "fall back" at the start of November, a shift from daylight saving time to standard time . The change has prompted political debate and criticism from President Donald Trump , who is calling on the Senate to pass the Sunshine Protection Act .

More than a dozen states want to make daylight saving time permanent , but can only do so with congressional approval.

So, how do you prepare your body for the change? Experts say adjust your sleep schedule, take advantage of morning sunlight, avoid consuming caffeine late at night and eat an earlier dinner.

Thinking ahead and dreading less daylight? Here's when time shifts forward in 2027.

When does daylight saving time begin in 2027?

Daylight saving time begins on Sunday, March 14, 2027, according to Time and Date . The clocks will spring forward from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m.

Daylight saving time is the period between March and November when most Americans adjust their clocks by one hour.

We lose an hour in March, instead of gaining an hour in the fall, to accommodate more daylight in the summer evenings. When we "fall back" in November, it's to add more daylight in the mornings.

The clock will change on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., going back to 1 a.m.

articles.title: A record number of health professionals are running for office. Could they help heal US politics?
articles.summary: At least 125 doctors, nurses and public health experts are on the ballot for Tuesday’s midterm elections — an unprecedented number from fields that historica...
articles.body:
At least 125 doctors, nurses and public health experts are on the ballot for Tuesday's midterm elections — an unprecedented number from fields that historically offered fewer paths to elected office than boardrooms and courtrooms.

Their campaigns emerged in the aftermath of Covid-19, when doctors and health officials were celebrated at first, overwhelmed by work and tragedy for years, and in some cases, targeted because of distrust or politics around their messages.

Some candidates say they realized during that time how their training and expertise in health and science were more closely tied to government and politics than they'd thought.

"One of the things you learn to do in medicine is to listen and sit with somebody in pain and help them to clarify what the opportunities are, based on your knowledge about how the body or their health works, and I find that the work of politics is really quite similar," said Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former health director for Wayne County, Michigan, who is running for US Senate against Republican Mike Rogers.

Dr. Amy Acton, a preventive medicine specialist who served as Republican Gov. Mike DeWine's high-profile public health director in Ohio, is running for governor as a Democrat against biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican.

Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former congressman who served as President Joe Biden's secretary of health and human services, is vying for the governor in California against Republican media personality Steve Hilton.

Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and pediatrician in South Carolina, is running for US Senate against Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

There are candidates with industry experience too, including healthcare attorney Cinde Warmington, a Democrat running to be New Hampshire's governor, and Republican Rick Jackson, founder and CEO of Jackson Healthcare, who's running to be Georgia's governor.

"I haven't seen anything exactly like this before," said historian Dr. Kristoffer Shields , director of the Eagleton Center on the American Governor at Rutgers University. "The link between science and politics has always been sort of weak."

Less than 10% of the current Congress has a medical, public health or engineering degree. By comparison, 47% of senators and 31% of House members have law degrees.

Congress does have tiny but active Republican and Democratic doctors' caucuses. Four people with health backgrounds — all Republicans and doctors — serve in the US Senate: Wyoming's John Barrasso, Louisiana's Bill Cassidy, Kansas' Roger Marshall and Kentucky's Rand Paul. The House has 17 physicians, four dentists, two pharmacists , a nurse practitioner , an optometrist and a rehabilitation therapist.

At the state level, the ranks are even thinner, and they've been shrinking. Only about 3% of state legislators had medical, science or engineering backgrounds as of March 2025, according to a Rutgers analysis of the Scientists in State Politics Database. That's down 25% from the year before.

Hawaii's Josh Green is the sole US governor with a medical degree, and no governors have a public health degree. No doctor has ever been president; the ninth president, William Henry Harrison, went to medical school but dropped out when he ran out of money to pay for it, and became a soldier instead.

Something seemed to change this year, said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, a political action committee that recruits, trains and helps Democrats with science, tech, engineering and math backgrounds get elected. His group has been flooded with support requests.

"We've had over 700 applications from people who want to run for office. To put that in context, it's usually been like 200 every election cycle," Polyak said.

The American Medical Association has long encouraged people in the profession to get involved in politics. It has two political education programs: a candidate workshop and a campaign school for members. Cassidy and Barrasso are graduates, as are US Reps. Ami Bera and Mariannette Miller-Meeks.

"Advocacy is strongest when physicians themselves are in the room where decisions are made. As is often noted, 'If you're not at the table, you're on the menu,'" AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in an email to CNN.

"More physicians running for office is a good sign. We don't think of ourselves as politicians, but we advocate for our patients every day because of prior authorization or other obstacles that prevent them from receiving care. We are accustomed to relentless advocacy."

Public health saw a similar surge in candidate interest.

"I started getting calls in January and February a year ago, asking me for advice," said Dr. Kristin Hook, a former staffer at the US National Institutes of Health and the US Government Accountability Office. She lost the first time she ran as a Democrat for Texas' 21st Congressional District, in 2024, but is on the ballot again this year for the same seat.

"People from all across the country wanted to run, and they wanted to know what I did and what I learned," she said. "I had these little chats with a bunch of public health folks, all different, and many former feds who wanted to prevent what we're seeing right now."

One strong motivator for Hook to run for office was what she sees as an attack on science by the Trump administration.

"Our country should be great. Our country should be pro-science, pro-innovation, and science keeps us safe. It protects us. It leads to wonderful discoveries, and this administration has completely burned all of that down," she said.

Hook points to the firing of thousands of federal doctors and scientists, cuts to billions in research funding, the removal of entire government datasets and public health websites, and the undermining of longstanding public health measures like water fluoridation and childhood vaccines .

Along with gas prices, healthcare is the biggest household expense worrying voters, polls show . Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill" is expected to cut insurance to 10 million more people , one of the biggest rollbacks in health insurance coverage ever, experts say .

Many of the candidates with healthcare backgrounds, like most Americans surveyed, say they disapprove of the current leadership at HHS.

"HHS is not a place for science deniers or science skeptics," Becerra told CNN earlier this year. "Why would you get rid of some of our best scientists and doctors and health professionals?

"I think it's a prescription for a real disaster," he added. "We deal with enough natural disasters, having to help with hurricanes, having to address pandemics, that's bad enough. But when you put on top of that these man-made disasters, then you know that America's health and America's economy are at risk."

The pandemic was also a major driver for many of the healthcare professionals now seeking office.

"They've been under heavy political fire and either survived it or have moved on and learned from it, and it's made them that much stronger," said Lori Tremmel Freeman, CEO of the National Association of County and City Health Officials.

Typically, public health leaders play a vital role that's out of the spotlight. But the pandemic pushed many onto everyone's television. For some, the attention brought death threats and hate mail, and a record number quit . Others emerged as local folk heroes.

Acton says she faced a handful of protesters at her home but mostly felt support from Ohioans, many of whom watched her daily briefings with DeWine, the Republican governor. During the pandemic, her image appeared on T-shirts and a mural, and a bobblehead ad quoted the Dayton Daily News describing her as "Ohio's trusted face during the pandemic." A 2020 New York Times editorial called Acton "the leader we wish we all had."

"The love in this state was so much greater than any of the hate," she said. "It was an honor to work alongside Gov. Mike DeWine. We were totally focused on saving lives, and we definitely put people's health and well-being over politics."

But it may be hard for public health leaders and doctors to win over voters aggrieved by pandemic-era vaccine policies, masking rules and shuttered schools and businesses.

"Especially on the Republican side, I think there's a lot more distrust of the medical profession post-Covid," said Woodrow Johnston, a political consultant for Republican politicians. "A lot of Republicans feel they were misled or even lied to when it came to government shutdowns."

Polls show that Democrats have more confidence in scientists than Republicans. However, one Pew poll found that trust dipped during the pandemic and has ticked up more recently. Another 2026 Pew survey found that scientists are more trusted to act in the public interest than journalists, business leaders and elected officials.

Not everyone realizes how much political skill public health leaders must wield to win support for their solutions, Freeman says. The pandemic tested many of them.

"We serve everyone everywhere in every single community, no matter what their political leaning," she said. "To have somebody with all of this wealth of experience in different areas would help all across the board, and not just health programs. Even just to help people understand that healthiness really drives economic prosperity."

Johnston said he has helped more Republican candidates with medical or public health backgrounds win office lately. Such candidates can connect with certain voters.

"Sometimes, smart people like smart people," Johnston said.

And their scientific expertise is needed, said Shields, the historian. Some problems are straightforward health issues, such as lack of access to care. Other problems are more existential: how to govern AI so it's safe, how to find renewable energy and how to address the climate crisis.

"There's so many issues that we're facing where we need people with scientific expertise in the room," he said.

Acton says that having health professionals in higher office can help people's health, perhaps even more than an individual doctor can help a patient. She thinks of the average lifespan in the US: Advances in medicine and technology account for some improvements, but a lot of it's also due to "things that we had to solve together."

"It was things like clean water, safe food, child labor laws, public school for every kid, traffic safety laws – the list goes on and on," Acton said. "That's what government's role is: a big catalyzer and convener."

She said it was clear to her while working with DeWine during Covid-19 that the governor's job was about protecting the health and well-being of everyone.

"Just like being a doctor, we're for all patients. Being governor is actually about improving those social and economic and environmental determinants of our well-being and our prosperity," Acton said. "It's funny. You think of it as so different, but I really realized it's actually exactly what I've been trained to do."
