articles.title: Judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit seeking to block Alaska Senate certification if GOP's Dan Sullivan loses
articles.summary: A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate race if GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, calling its...
articles.body:
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, two days before Election Day.

U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote that the relief the government sought was "infeasible" because many ballots have already been cast and mixed together, the AP reported . She also wrote that the government "provides no workable plan" for separating ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan and investigating them "in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy."

Gleason found the federal government did not have the ability to bring the case, NPR reported . Justice Department attorneys are expected to appeal, according to NPR. The ruling does not end the criminal investigation into how the second Sullivan got on the ballot.

It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska.

One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .)

But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department sued last month in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes.

Then, on Oct. 28, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot."

"The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory."

Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity.

In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social .

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law.

"Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections."

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2002, wrote in a statement that the people of her state deserve a full explanation.

"Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments," she wrote. "By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong."

Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election.

"Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation."

Rep. James Comer, the Republican head of the House Oversight Committee, said Oct. 29 that the committee is "taking action" to launch an investigation into the matter, including an inquiry into whether any crimes may have been committed. ABC News also reported Oct. 29 that the DOJ had issued a wave of new subpoenas as it probes whether the alleged recruitment scheme may have run afoul of federal conspiracy laws.

On Friday, Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for Alaska, confirmed there is a criminal investigation, saying it had been underway for months. He said the Times report led to a "significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, but declined to say what crimes are being examined and said he was "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed," according to CBS News .

Before the ruling, the Justice Department had also asked Gleason to order state officials to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan" so it could investigate possible voter confusion, and it requested action before Monday . State attorneys had asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the ballot already distinguishes the two men. It lists the senator as Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican and the incumbent, and the challenger as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party, the AP reported .

In a filing Saturday, Alaska's Republican-run government urged Gleason to dismiss the case, calling it a "meritless lawsuit" and the ballot request "both disturbing and impossible" because it couldn't be carried out without violating voter privacy, the AP reported . "Not every wrong can be righted in federal court," the state wrote. The Trump administration says it is trying to combat fraud.

On Friday, a federal appeals court rejected a similar DOJ request in California to set aside disputed ballots.

An FBI agent also visited the Petersburg business of a Sullivan donor to ask whether he had been misled, the AP reported . The donor said he hadn't. "Everybody knows who the incumbent is," he said.

At a rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., on Friday, Trump said Peltola "should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted," adding that Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision, MS NOW reported . No one has been charged.

Peltola said at a rally in Anchorage that she was "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." Asked whether someone on her campaign could have been involved, she told KTUU, "I honestly have no idea." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement, and Dan J. Sullivan has long denied running at Democrats' behest.

On CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Sen. Sullivan said he doubted Peltola's denials. "There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," he said. Asked about certification, he said, "I'm going to accept the results of the election."

Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who leads the GOP's Senate campaign arm, said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that criminal charges might make sense. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent of Vermont, said on CBS' "Face the Nation" that what Democrats did "seems to me to be pretty dumb," adding, "It's not illegal."

Dunleavy, the Republican governor, suggested his state investigation could still affect the outcome. "If we find out there's wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that's what happens," he told NewsNation on Friday.

The outcome of the fight could still have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a move to block or erase a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency.

How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story.

How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot

Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal."

But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report .

How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ).

For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name.

The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two."

But according to the Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages.

For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication.

The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort.

Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last month. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot.

"Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing.

"I'm the one that said do it," Trump said last month of the lawsuit.

The suit argued that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead.

Democrats asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, also moved to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Oct. 26, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day.

Before Gleason's ruling, many legal experts said the lawsuit had a slim chance of success. First, it required a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts said, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters did not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected.

"I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon .

Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures.

"The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said.

More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections.

"This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media .

Voters decide the race Tuesday. The Justice Department is expected to appeal Gleason's ruling, while the federal criminal investigation, Dunleavy's state investigation and the House Oversight Committee's inquiry continue.

An appeal would likely only matter in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans.

Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat."

articles.title: Texas Poll Shows Talarico Leading Paxton, Governor's Race Dead Heat
articles.summary: Texas Poll: Talarico Leading Paxton; Governor's Race Dead Heat
articles.body:
Democrats are showing unexpected strength in Texas just days before Tuesday's midterm elections, with new polling indicating a competitive Senate race, a virtual tie for governor, and substantial support for Democrat candidates among Hispanic voters.

A YouGov survey conducted Oct. 26-29 showed Democrat Senate candidate James Talarico leading Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton 51% to 47%, a 4-percentage-point lead compared with a 3-point margin in an earlier University of Texas poll.

Meanwhile, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott leads Democrat challenger Gina Hinojosa just 50% to 49%, suggesting an unusually competitive gubernatorial contest in a state Republicans have dominated for decades.

The YouGov survey questioned 2,141 likely Texas voters and had a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points, meaning Abbott's 1-point lead was within the margin of error.

Other recent surveys also showed competitive races, although the margins varied.

A YouGov Blue poll conducted for 254 Labs showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 43%, while Hinojosa led Abbott 49% to 46%.

An N+ Univision/YouGov survey released Oct. 27 showed Talarico leading Paxton 50% to 45%, while Abbott led Hinojosa 48% to 46%.

The tightening contests coincide with a major increase in voter participation.

More than 7.4 million Texans cast early ballots, representing 39% of registered voters, according to preliminary figures reported by The Texas Tribune.

By comparison, 5.5 million Texans voted early in the 2022 midterms, while the latest figures approached the early-voting turnout rate recorded in 2018.

Hispanic voters accounted for a larger share of early ballots than in previous elections.

An analysis of the first week of early voting found that Hispanic voters accounted for 18% of ballots cast compared with 17% in 2024 and 16% in 2022.

Democrat strategists say increased turnout in heavily Hispanic communities could influence several competitive races, although early-voting demographics don't reveal how individuals voted.

Polling suggests Democrats have substantial support among Hispanic voters.

The N+ Univision survey showed Talarico leading Paxton 55% to 37% among Hispanic voters.

Hinojosa led Abbott 52% to 43% among Hispanic voters.

The survey also found regional differences, with Republicans performing better among Hispanic voters in North Texas and Democrats drawing stronger support in Central and South Texas.

The survey also highlighted concerns about household finances and immigration enforcement.

The Univision poll found that 42% of Hispanic respondents reported worsening household finances, while 56% said immigration enforcement had gone too far.

Despite the close polling and increased early voting, the outcomes of both races remain uncertain.

Texas voters do not register by political party, making early-vote trends difficult to interpret.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro recorre contra apreensão de passaportes; defesa pede que Moraes seja declarado impedido em investigação  | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro descumpriu a ordem dada pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, e fugiu do país. O senador, sua esposa e as filhas do casal chegaram aos Estados Unidos na última quarta-feira (28).
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro descumpriu a ordem dada pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, e fugiu do país. O senador, sua esposa e as filhas do casal chegaram aos Estados Unidos na última quarta-feira (28).
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca nos EUA — Foto: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Reuters

A defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), derrotado nas eleições presidenciais, pediu a revogação da decisão do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), que determinou no domingo (25) a entrega de seus passaportes.

Na mesma decisão, Moraes também determinou a proibição de contato entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Willer Tomaz e o cancelamento de todos os passaportes brasileiros, incluindo o diplomático.

Flávio Bolsonaro descumpriu a ordem de Moraes e fugiu do país. O senador, sua esposa e as filhas do casal chegaram aos Estados Unidos na última quarta-feira (28). O avião utilizado pela família pousou em um aeroporto de Miami, na Flórida.

Decisão em investigação por lavagem de dinheiro

A decisão de Moraes foi dada em processo em que Flávio Bolsonaro e o advogado Willer Tomaz são investigados por lavagem de dinheiro , em um suposto esquema que envolve empresas de Tomaz e bets.

Essa investigação começou na primeira instância da Justiça Federal no Rio Grande do Sul, onde eram apurados crimes como lavagem de dinheiro, evasão de divisas e a utilização de casas de apostas no suposto esquema.

O caso foi levado ao STF após o nome de Flávio Bolsonaro aparecer nas apurações da Polícia Federal (PF) gaúcha.

Flávio Bolsonaro também é formalmente investigado em inquérito aberto para apurar a possível prática de crimes relacionados ao financiamento da produção do filme "Dark Horse" , sobre a trajetória do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

Os advogados de Flávio Bolsonaro pediram ainda que a investigação, que tem ele e Willer Tomaz como alvos, saia das mãos de Moraes e seja redistribuída ao ministro André Mendonça.

O argumento da defesa é que a estrutura atribuída a Willer Tomaz, a hipótese de lavagem de dinheiro e a eventual prática do crime de organização criminosa já são objeto de outra investigação no âmbito da Operação Sem Desconto, que apura um esquema de fraudes no INSS, sob relatoria de Mendonça.

A defesa solicitou ainda que Moraes seja declarado impedido para conduzir a investigação, ou alternativamente, ou seja declarado suspeito para continuar à frente do caso.

Para os advogados de Flávio Bolsonaro, Moraes não pode atuar em investigação que tem a Fraction 024 como parte de apuração em virtude de aparentes vínculos objetivos, documentados e públicos, entre a empresa, o escritório de advocacia de sua esposa Viviane Barci de Moraes e o próprio ministro.

A aeronave usada por Flávio Bolsonaro era gerida pela Prime Aviation, empresa ligada ao ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, em contrato de 10 anos de cessão com a Fraction 024.

articles.title: Durigan nega discussão sobre tabelamento de juros no governo Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro da Fazenda também afirma que não há encontro previsto entre Lula e André Lara Resende, um dos pais do Plano Real e defensor de um novo arranjo entre políticas fiscal e monetária para reduzir a taxa Selic.
articles.summary: Dario Durigan e Mercadante negam propostas para tabelar a taxa Selic ou usar reservas cambiais e desmentem reunião entre Lula e o economista André Lara Resende.
articles.body:
O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, negou que esteja em avaliação para o quarto mandato do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) propostas como tabelar juros da taxa Selic ou queimar reservas cambiais para compensar eventual saída de capitais do Brasil.

O posicionamento do ministro vem depois que interlocutores de Lula repercutiram a possibilidade de o presidente se encontrar nesta semana com o economista André Lara Resende, um dos pais do Plano Real e defensor da proposta ( veja mais detalhes abaixo ).

A informação de que haveria essa reunião foi publicada pelo jornal O Globo. Segundo Durigan, no entanto, não há agenda prevista entre Lula e Resende.

"Vários economistas estão se colocando à disposição para dialogar com o presidente [Lula] e com o presidente do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), Aloizio Mercadante, mas não há nada agendado. Não há agenda com o presidente Lula e o economista André Lara Resende", disse o ministro.

Mercadante é um histórico aliado de Lula e atuou como conselheiro na campanha deste ano do petista ao Planalto principalmente em temas ligados à política econômica.

Na campanha do petista de 2022, ele foi responsável por elaborar o plano de governo de Lula. Já na transição, coordenou os mais de 30 grupos técnicos de trabalho.

Mercadante também negou que as propostas de André Lara estejam em discussão no governo e que haja um eventual encontro agendado do economista com Lula.

"Não há nenhuma proposta de tabelar juros em discussão, não teve na campanha e não tem no governo. Vamos aguardar o presidente definir a equipe econômica. A campanha já terminou, agora o presidente coordena o processo e define as responsabilidades", disse Mercadante ao g1.

"O governo Lula sempre governou assegurando transparência e previsibilidade da política econômica. O presidente precisa definir as responsabilidades pela economia e caberá a nova equipe construir as equipes e estabelecer os diálogos".

Segundo Mercadante, o presidente Lula vai começar a discutir o quarto mandato a partir desta terça-feira (3).

Após derrotar Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na disputa presidencial , Lula se manteve recolhido no Palácio da Alvorada e nos últimos dias na Residência Oficial na Granja do Torto para descansar e recompor a voz.

Dario Durigan, Ministro da Fazenda do Brasil, fala durante uma entrevista à Reuters em Pequim, China. — Foto: Maxim Shemetov / Reuters

Em uma publicação feita no fim de setembro, André Lara Resende propõe um novo arranjo entre as políticas fiscal e monetária para reduzir a taxa Selic.

O plano do economista também prevê a criação de um Conselho Fiscal e Monetário Nacional, que definiria metas fiscais e monetárias para um período de quatro a cinco anos à frente.

"O BC se comprometeria a manter a taxa básica num intervalo entre a meta de inflação, 3,0%, e taxa de crescimento nominal potencial, ou seja, a meta da inflação somada ao crescimento real potencial, o que hoje seria em torno de 5,5% ao ano (3% de inflação mais 2,5% de crescimento)", diz a proposta.

"Para dar início ao novo regime fiscal e monetário, o BC anunciaria a redução gradual do juro básico, ao longo de cerca de 12 meses, para a taxa de crescimento nominal potencial mais um spread transitório de segurança de 2%, isto é, perto de 7,5% ao ano. Este spread de segurança seria periodicamente reavaliado e gradualmente reduzido até ser eliminado", propõe o economista.

No texto, o economista critica a alta da taxa de juros. A taxa Selic está atualmente em 13,75% ao ano , definida pelo Comitê de Política Monetária (Copom) do Banco Central.

"A economia tem um problema básico: a extraordinariamente alta taxa básica de juros. Um problema que tem solução clara. Só é preciso vencer os preconceitos associados a uma teoria monetária e fiscal anacrônica", afirma Resende.

Em uma postagem nas redes sociais, Gleisi Hoffmann (PT-PR), deputada federal e ex-ministra das Relações Instituicionais de Lula, defendeu o artigo do economista e afirmou que a publicação é "fundamental para enfrentar a ofensiva sobre a política fiscal brasileira".

Em uma outra publicação nesta segunda-feira (2), Gleisi criticou a repercussão negativa no mercado financeiro do possível encontro de Lula com Resende e afirmou que "o mercado financeiro tem o DNA do autoritarismo".

"Parece normal que o presidente Lula chame para conversar gente que não está tão comprometida com essa Faria Lima. Até porque, conversar e procurar entender todos os problemas é uma virtude do presidente. Isso não quer dizer que esses adversários não tenham entendido ainda que Lula não fará o estelionato eleitoral que defendem, alguns em voz alta e com todas as letras", afirmou a ex-ministra.

articles.title: Ranked Choice Voting Will Untangle Alaska's Dan Sullivan Controversy. It's Also on the Ballot Itself.
articles.summary: As voters in Alaska decide whether to keep or abolish some electoral reforms, voters in Massachusetts will decide whether to try them.
articles.body:
An underappreciated facet of the controversy that has rocked the Alaska Senate race: Voting reforms adopted by the state in 2020 will likely blunt the effectiveness of an apparent Democratic scheme to place a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

And an additional twist: Voters in the state have a chance to undo those election reforms on Tuesday night.

Alaskans may determine which party controls the Senate, but the race has been complicated by a second candidate with nearly the same name as incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan (R–Alaska). The New York Times reported last week that Democratic challenger Mary Peltola's campaign was behind the maneuver to get Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, on the ballot .

Peltola denies the accusation, but the Times ' reporting looks sound, and the potential impact seems clear—the incumbent may lose some share of votes meant for him because voters mistakenly tab the wrong Sullivan. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to block the certification of results in the race preemptively.

The scheme is playing out against the backdrop of Alaska's unusual electoral system. The state has an open primary , and its top four vote-getters then advance to the general election—a model more similar to a "regular season" and "playoffs" format familiar to sports fans than to the process most states use.

In the primary round, held in August, Peltola and the incumbent Sullivan were the clear frontrunners. The other Sullivan finished third. The fourth-place finisher, a Democrat, withdrew from the general election and was replaced on the ballot by the fifth-place finisher, Republican Gerald Heikes.

Critics of the top-four primary might see this controversy as an indictment of that electoral reform model. After all, the second Sullivan may not have been on the general election ballot if there had been a more typical partisan primary that could have eliminated him.

That conclusion, however, misses the other half of Alaska's new electoral system. The general election uses ranked choice voting to determine a winner. That ought to limit the second Sullivan's ability to sway the outcome.

To illustrate why, let's assume for the sake of argument that every single vote cast for Daniel J. Sullivan is an accident. He got 2.5 percent in the primary, so let's also assume that he repeats that performance. Voters who are confused by the two Sullivans are likely to list the incumbent, Daniel S. Sullivan, as their second choice on the ranked choice ballot.

As the votes are tallied , the candidate with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated, and his or her ballots are redistributed according to voters' second choice. When one Sullivan is eliminated , you'd expect most of his votes to be reallocated to the other Sullivan.

Not every confused voter will list both Sullivans. But without the ranked choice system, he'd lose all of that 2.5 percent of the vote. Thanks to Alaska's ranked choice system , the effect will be much smaller .

Of course, Peltola may get an outright majority on the first round of counting, as she nearly did in the primary. If so, then Sullivan has nothing to complain about. He would have lost no matter how the votes are counted.

Amid all this controversy, Alaskans are also deciding this week whether to keep those electoral reforms. Ballot Measure 2 asks voters if they want to repeal the current voting system and revert to the old model of partisan primaries and first-past-the-post general elections.

Both President Donald Trump and Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy have campaigned for the repeal. Many top state officials oppose the ballot measure , as does the Libertarian Party of Alaska .

On the other side of the country, voters in Massachusetts are also being asked about election reforms on this year's ballot. Question 3 , if approved, would eliminate party primaries for statewide offices and implement a single ballot primary, with the top two candidates in the primary round advancing to the general election.

A top-two primary versus a top-four primary (as Alaska uses) would eliminate the sort of shenanigans that the Peltola campaign has allegedly tried to pull. On the other hand, a top-two primary effectively freezes out smaller parties and independent candidates—as has happened in California since the state adopted that model in 2011.

There is no perfect way to run an election , and no way to eliminate political gamesmanship. Despite becoming a lightning rod for controversy this year, the ranked choice approach is part of the solution, not the problem.

articles.title: Mamdani, Hasan Piker among radical left-wing voices erupting over Haley Stevens' endorsement switch
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries and top Democrats unleashed fury at Haley Stevens after her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers before Tuesday.
articles.body: Prominent Democrats and left-wing voices nationwide exploded with fury after Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in the final stretch of Michigan's U.S. Senate race over the weekend. In her video posted to social media on Sunday after attending church service with Rogers, Stevens noted how Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed told her to "stay away" from his campaign and slammed him for embracing radical steamer Hasan Piker — who was among those criticizing the endorsement. "Working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday—their healthcare, their rent, their bills," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in an X post. "Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against." Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said on X shortly after the endorsement: "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT Stevens, who will leave Congress in January, lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year. She was widely viewed as the moderate, establishment candidate compared to the more progressive, left-wing policies of her opponent. On Sunday, Stevens abandoned the party in the final hours of the Senate campaign as Democrats seek to win back control of the upper chamber. "This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said on X. "Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors." DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH "Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return." Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., called Stevens "clearly disturbed," and said she "has thrown her constituents under the bus" on several key midterm issues. HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION' "Too many people live off their 15 minutes of fame," Pocan continued. "In this case, she threw away an entire career because she couldn’t get over a loss and needed attention. Pathetic. Sad. Clearly she has some serious issues. But no one will take her seriously ever again." Outside of her own colleagues condemning her endorsement, Stevens also saw an immediate staff exodus after she posted the video. After the endorsement, a visibly upset El-Sayed demanded the media focus their questions on political issues, rather than Stevens' endorsement. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS "I'm going to ask that when we take questions, you keep your questions focused on the issues that Michiganders really care about. Now that might not drive clicks for you. I get it. I understand your business, right? But they're the issues that Michiganders are paying attention to," he said. FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY Stevens drew an official condemnation from the Democratic Party at a national level, too. "Haley Stevens’ disappointing decision to endorse Mike Rogers, a Trump ally who would join Republican efforts to sell out working families, is a betrayal of the values of the Democratic Party," Democratic National Committee (DNC) chairman Ken Martin said in a statement on behalf of the organization. "At a moment when Democrats are united in fighting for Michigan families and standing up to Trump’s agenda, we reject these efforts to sow division within our party. We will not allow last-minute political stunts to derail our momentum and we will triple down on our efforts to elect Abdul El-Sayed on Tuesday." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), chaired by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., lashed out at Stevens' decision, too. MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED "The stakes of this election could not be higher: Mike Rogers is a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, and together they plan to continue sowing chaos and making life unaffordable for families while prioritizing their billionaire donors at the expense of Michigan families," the DSCC statement said, adding the group will "reject any efforts to divide Democrats ahead of Tuesday’s crucial election." DEMOCRAT RIPS HASAN PIKER AS 'HACK WHO THRIVES ON HATE' OVER HIS WARNING TO AMERICAN JEWS ABOUT ISRAEL Piker, who was partly the reason for Stevens' break from El-Sayed, simply wrote: "i [sic] condemn haley stevens." Piker has caused major controversy in the Michigan race due to his proximity to El-Sayed. Since his primary win, the progressive candidate has sought to distance himself from the streamer. "This is the single most unproductive, selfish thing a Democratic candidate has done all cycle and likely many cycles before that," Jon Favreau, Pod Save America cohost and speechwriter to President Barack Obama, said on X. "Having misjudged candidates in the past myself, I hope everyone who tried to recruit, support, and defend Haley can now admit what a mistake it was." HALEY STEVENS URGES EL-SAYED TO DITCH HASAN PIKER AFFILIATION AFTER MICHIGAN PRIMARY Fellow PodSaveAmerica cohost Jon Lovett called Stevens a "sleaze." "Not to downplay Haley Stevens' vermin-like betrayal of her party and her constituents and her nation... But given her track record as a clownish loser, do we really believe any who will now follow her weren't already going to vote for the Fascist?" podcaster and former television sports personality Keith Olbermann said in an X post. Stevens, who was narrowly defeated by El-Sayed in Michigan's Aug. 4, 2026 primary election, crossed partisan lines after saying for months that she would support El-Sayed. It all devolved after Stevens expressed concern last week over an ad aired in El-Sayed's favor that was widely viewed as antisemitic. She said she would appear at a weekend campaign event with El-Sayed on the condition that he denounced the ad. El-Sayed, whose support among the Michigan Jewish community is already tenuous, disinvited her from the event instead. The ad that sparked the controversy was released by the Rebellion PAC, which is operated by The Young Turks co-founder and bombastic leftist commentator Cenk Uygur, who is Piker's uncle. Piker, whom El-Sayed invited onto the campaign trail in Michigan during primary season, has been a headache for El-Sayed during the general election. Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets, and is known for making antisemitic comments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed has refused to denounce Piker, brushing him off as a "streamer from California" who he says shouldn't be the focus of the campaign in Michigan.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots from people the...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots from people the federal government claims are noncitizens, a decision that came hours before the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections .

The high court refused to immediately intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state's voter rolls.

The swift rejection capped a string of losses for the president's effort to intervene in the election before the counting of ballots to decide who controls Congress in the last two years of his second term. No justices publicly dissented.

Several lower courts also rejected the Justice Department's push to set aside the challenged California ballots until the voters' citizenship status could be verified. In Alaska, a judge did not even hold a hearing before dismissing a Trump-ordered suit to prevent a possible Democratic Senate win.

The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump's push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.

The Republican administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare. California officials said the administration's list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.

Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration's efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution.

"The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone," Chief Judge James Boasberg wrote.

The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.

The administration's push has faced a remarkable series of losses in court, as well as criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable.

During a hearing over whether to lift her own order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department's data.

"Would you agree there's a high error rate?" Thompson asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney.

"That's a fair statement," Kao said. "That's why we ask for the registrars' aid in verifying these are all valid voters."

At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department's Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote.

"This isn't speculation. This isn't a theory," Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list.

Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state's roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law."

Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.

A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California's unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the "violation of federal law."

The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.

Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento, California, and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

articles.title: DOJ appeals to Supreme Court to reverse block on segregating 20K California ballots
articles.summary: The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block rulings denying its bid to segregate over 20,000 California mail-in ballots.
articles.body: The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block lower-court rulings that denied its request to segregate more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots cast by people it says are likely not U.S. citizens, hours before a federal judge ruled against the Trump administration on the matter. The DOJ argues the limited injunction would preserve the ballots while their eligibility is investigated, without canceling any votes. California and the federal government dispute whether the ballots are unlawful. "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy," the Justice Department wrote in a court filing. JUDGE REJECTS DOJ REQUEST TO BLOCK CALIFORNIA FROM IMMEDIATELY COUNTING BALLOTS LINKED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the request Friday, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting, as did a federal judge in Los Angeles last week. The case remains under review, and the DOJ is seeking relief while the matter proceeds. California says its safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and argues the federal list may contain errors that could disenfranchise eligible voters. The lower courts also cited the state’s authority over election procedures and warned that granting the request could jeopardize the election. On Monday evening, a federal judge in Washington D.C., it was "likely" the Trump administration violated the Constitution by taking over responsibilities for elections from the states and Congress. Chief Judge James Boasberg issued an injunction blocking the administration from making requests of California over its mail ballots. DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS The case stems from an Oct. 15 Justice Department lawsuit alleging that California is impeding enforcement of a federal law barring noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The administration says the state violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which generally gives federal law precedence over state law. The dispute comes amid the administration’s broader push to influence how states run elections, including demands for access to voter rolls and warnings that officials could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. articles.body: The leader of one of the nation’s oldest and largest unions stunned political observers by issuing a surprise endorsement for a Senate Republican stalwart over the weekend. Teamsters General President Sean O’Brien, who famously nearly came to blows with now-Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin during a Senate hearing before ultimately becoming acquaintances, issued a ringing endorsement of Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., signaling a major break from national union sentiment that has tended to favor Democrats. "Just voted in the State of Florida for the first time, and very proud to have cast a ballot for Sen. Ashley Moody," O’Brien, whose 123-year-old union is about 1.3 million-strong, announced Sunday. 5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON "Sen. Moody has been extremely helpful working with the Teamsters to protect workers’ pensions, defend good-paying jobs, and support well-funded union apprenticeship programs." "The Teamsters look forward to working with Sen. Moody in her role on the Senate HELP Committee to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act and get this critical legislation signed into law to protect American workers," he added. FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY O’Brien, a self-described "lifelong Democrat," previously spoke at the 2024 Republican National Convention, but emphasized at the time that the Democratic Party had snubbed his request to speak at its convention. articles.title: Federal Judge Dismisses DOJ Lawsuit Over Alaska Senate Race, Calling Proposed Remedy 'Infeasible'
articles.summary: Democrats almost certainly engaged in dirty tricks, but to most any politician's relief, being underhanded is not illegal.
articles.body:
On the eve of the midterms, it may be a bit of a surprise that the Alaska Senate race would be a focus of national attention.

But along with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, the ballot will include two other candidates, including a second Dan Sullivan—retired schoolteacher Daniel J. Sullivan.

For months, the latter Sullivan insisted he was a sincere candidate running for a seat in Congress' upper chamber, and sharing a name with the sitting senator was simply a coincidence and not an intentional attempt to siphon votes.

That story fell apart last week, when The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign and Democratic Party strategists had actively recruited candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan, to stack the ballot against the Republican senator.

After the Times report, President Donald Trump said Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan "should be prosecuted." Gov. Mike Dunleavy wrote on X that he had directed state authorities "to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) had already sued, asking the state not to certify the results of the election if the senator lost by a narrow enough margin that it could conceivably have stemmed from confusion over two Dan Sullivans. After the Times piece appeared, the DOJ amended its complaint to include the new revelations.

The Peltola campaign's dirty tricks are certainly disreputable. But to most any politician's relief, being underhanded is not illegal, nor is misleading or even outright lying to voters.

Besides, the government's lawsuit had a number of problems, leading a federal judge to throw it out over the weekend.

"Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan," the Justice Department's filing warned , "the State and its officers will fail in their obligations to protect the integrity of its election and obstruct Congress's purposes and objectives in enacting various election integrity laws."

For the remedy, it requested that the court "enjoin Defendants from certifying any result" in which Sullivan lost by too narrow a margin, "pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."

The DOJ had to contend with Purcell v. Gonzalez , a 2006 decision in which the U.S. Supreme Court cautioned against issuing "court orders affecting elections" too close to Election Day. Whatever remedy the government sought, it would have to get around that proscription.

"The requested relief here would not change the rules of the election," the government explained in an amended complaint . "It would merely require preservation and segregation of potentially tainted ballots, and only if the result may have been impacted by the scheme to confuse voters, pending an investigation."

In other words, if Sullivan (or, presumably, Peltola) did not win by a wide enough margin, the DOJ said the state should set aside all ballots that voted for the other Sullivan and conduct some sort of (unspecified) investigation into whether those voters actually intended to vote for the senator.

"Delaying certification of Alaska's election results—but only if a particular candidate does not win—would interfere with state election administration and threaten election integrity," Alaska officials replied in a motion to dismiss . "Worse, the United States contemplates an open-ended 'investigation' that would violate ballot secrecy."

The DOJ's purported investigation, the Alaskan filing added, "would require segregating ballots cast for Daniel J. and identifying them with the voters who cast them, so that those voters could later be interrogated about their intent. But that is not possible. Like every state in the union, Alaska protects the secrecy of the ballot by law, and such an investigation would require violating that secrecy."

In an opinion issued Sunday, Judge Sharon L. Gleason of the U.S. District Court of Alaska agreed.

"Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violate Alaskans' right to a secret ballot," Gleason wrote . "This Court lacks the authority to order that certain ballots cast by Alaskans be segregated so that federal law enforcement officials can conduct an unspecified investigation of the voters who cast them."

"The relief requested here by the United States is 'infeasible,'" Gleason concluded.

For those reasons, as well as the government's inability to give a justification strong enough to get past the Purcell principle, Gleason dismissed the lawsuit, finding that the courts did not have the authority to grant the DOJ's request.

Even if the lawsuit had gotten past those hurdles, it still would have faced an uphill climb.

For one thing, the DOJ explained its authority on the issue by citing the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (NVRA), noting that "Congress has tasked state officials with 'protect[ing] the integrity of the electoral process.'"

But as the UCLA law professor Richard L. Hasen notes , that clause appears in the act's preamble and does not contain any operative phrases that actually grant rights or authorities.

"If Congress intended to give the federal government these breathtaking powers over states—contrary to American history and tradition—it would not hide such an intent in the preamble of a statute about voter registration," Hasen wrote in an amicus brief. "The plain meaning of the NVRA's preamble gives the United States executive branch no powers over state and local election processes."

All evidence suggests that Daniel J. Sullivan—with the assistance of Democrats—did in fact jump into the race solely to draw votes away from Dan Sullivan, the sitting senator. But that doesn't mean it's illegal to do so. If we could keep people from running for office based solely on the worthiness of their intentions, that would essentially let those in power pick who is allowed to run against them.

articles.title: Minnesota reports record midterm early voting turnout
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Minnesota is reporting record-high turnout during early voting, with more residents casting ballots before Election Day than in any pre...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Minnesota is reporting record-high turnout during early voting, with more residents casting ballots before Election Day than in any previous midterm election.

As of Nov. 2, nearly 900,000 Minnesotans have already cast their ballots. With nearly 4 million registered voters statewide, that means roughly one in four has voted early.

"Early voting in Minnesota is sky-high," said Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon.

Mail-in voting began Sept. 18, while in-person early voting started Oct. 16. As of Nov. 2, the Minnesota secretary of state's website reported 266,580 mail-in ballots and 619,847 in-person ballots accepted, for a combined total of 886,427 ballots.

The current total far exceeds early voting numbers in previous midterm elections, when 687,062 ballots were returned in 2022 and 652,053 in 2018.

The 886,427 ballots also surpass the 689,228 cast early during the 2016 general election.

Minnesota first introduced no-excuse absentee voting in 2014, allowing voters to cast ballots early without providing a reason.

Simon is predicting continued "really high" turnout going into Election Day.

This comes as immigration policy, concerns over widespread fraud and the high cost of living take center stage in the North Star State.

articles.title: El-Sayed, Michigan Democrats push to galvanize voters after stunning Senate race defection
articles.summary: (AP) — Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and fellow Michigan Democrats scrambled Monday to refocus attention on turning out Election Day voters after his former...
articles.body:
WEST BLOOMFIELD TOWNSHIP, Mich. (AP) — Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and fellow Michigan Democrats scrambled Monday to refocus attention on turning out Election Day voters after his former primary rival stunned the party by endorsing the Republican candidate in one of the country's most closely watched races.

The final push before Tuesday's midterms followed a dramatic Sunday, when Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after appearing alongside him at church. It prompted her expulsion from the state Democratic Party and drew fierce condemnation from party leaders and longtime allies.

El-Sayed made no mention of the controversy at an event Monday morning at Eastern Michigan University, instead emphasizing that his campaign was about voters, not himself. Asked afterward what he would tell supporters nervous about the impact of Stevens' endorsement on the race, El-Sayed had a simple message: "Go vote."

"There's only one thing we can do to control the outcome," he added. He was joined at Monday's rally by Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and his grandparents, who greeted the crowd.

With over 2.3 million Michigan voters having already cast their ballots as of Monday, the question is whether the extraordinary political drama will matter to those who have yet to vote. Nearly 4.5 million people voted in the 2022 midterms. The state's regular early in-person voting period ended Sunday, with polls reopening statewide Tuesday.

"Well, around half of people have already voted," said Lori Goldman, a longtime Democratic organizer in Oakland County, a party stronghold near Detroit. "But for the rest, it could matter a hell of a lot."

On Monday, Associated Press reporters spoke to voters throughout Stevens' congressional district to hear their reactions. Stevens predominately represents Oakland County, home to West Bloomfield, Bloomfield Hills, Royal Oak and a large Jewish population.

Derryl Reed, who lives in Stevens' district and voted for her in the primary, even attending her election watch party, said he was disappointed.

"I see it mobilizing people to support Abdul more because they're so pissed off," said Reed. "She's gone back on her word."

Cassaundra Sims, a 62-year-old resident of West Bloomfield who voted for Stevens in the past, described her reaction to the Rogers endorsement as "Shocking, surprising and, frankly, disappointing."

"For her to be there supporting him, she has clearly shown us that she is not for us and that she is not somebody that we can trust," Sims, who is Black, said of Stevens' past support from the Black community.

Brian Butler of Bloomfield Hills, who has already voted but declined to say for whom, said he believed "Haley did the right thing."

"I think the Jewish people have been terribly treated and she wasn't going to put up with it," he said.

For Rogers and Republicans, the endorsement represented a remarkable political coup . Rogers personally reached out to Stevens over the weekend, according to a person with direct knowledge of the discussions. Even Rogers' own staff was unaware of the planned joint appearance at Perfecting Church until Sunday morning and learned of Stevens' endorsement only when it was posted online, the person said. The campaign was touting the endorsement to voters Monday.

For Democrats, the defection exposed lingering divisions over El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated Stevens in a bruising primary marked by disagreements over Israel and the war in Gaza. Party leaders had spent the final weeks of the campaign trying to shore up support for El-Sayed, particularly among Jewish and Black voters who had strongly backed Stevens.

Those leaders rebuked Stevens and said it would only energize their base. El-Sayed reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, his largest fundraising day of the campaign, while the state party said it saw a surge of people volunteering to knock on doors.

"I don't think this changes the election results other than it galvanizes Democrats," said Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel.

Stevens is rebuked by former supporters and critics alike

Michigan Democrats for months were divided on which candidate to support in the August primary, when El-Sayed defeated Stevens by around 14,000 votes. But in the weeks since, many have rallied around El-Sayed as the party's nominee.

Goldman, who supported Stevens in her first congressional campaign and has known her for a decade, said she was shocked by the reversal.

"I think she's thrown away a career that had import," Goldman said. "I'm stunned. And I feel a little heartbroken for her."

Debbie Rosenman, who leads two Democratic organizations in southeast Michigan, an area Stevens has partially represented in Congress for years, said the endorsement had left local Democrats feeling betrayed.

"What I am hearing is fury," Rosenman said. "They are just infuriated with her and feel betrayed by her."

Adrian Hemond, a Democratic strategist who supported Stevens and has been so critical of El-Sayed that he plans to leave the Senate race blank, said the congresswoman's endorsement had nothing to do with their policy differences: "If it did, she would have done it a month ago."

"This is colossally stupid. But it has zero to do with any substance. It has to do with personal animosity between these two," Hemond said.

Soon after her primary loss, Stevens endorsed El-Sayed, saying she would do "whatever he wants me to do" on the campaign trail. But she remained absent from the campaign trail for months, something that became increasingly noticeable as Jewish leaders criticized El-Sayed.

El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of Israel, and has been criticized for a statement in which he said "hurt people hurt people" after a synagogue attack and for appearing with controversial streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail.

Those controversies largely preceded Stevens' endorsement of El-Sayed. He has since apologized for his comments following the synagogue attack and has not appeared with Piker again. But Stevens and some Jewish leaders have maintained that he has not done enough to address their concerns. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, said last week that he would vote for Rogers.

The tensions came to a head over a planned Sunday unity event featuring Stevens and El-Sayed. After their public sparring over Israel and an outside group's campaign advertisement threatened to overshadow the gathering, Rep. Debbie Dingell, a senior Michigan Democratic figure close to Stevens, said she uninvited the congresswoman because the dispute had become "distracting."

Dingell and other Democrats said Stevens had repeatedly reassured them that the dispute would not cause her to withdraw her support for El-Sayed.

Few anticipated what would happen Sunday morning, when Stevens sat beside Rogers in church and announced her endorsement of the Republican shortly afterward.

"This is about Abdul getting angrier and angrier and saying, 'I don't want these people in my campaign,'" Stevens said later in a CNN interview. "This is a weight off my shoulders."

Dingell, visibly shaken during a CNN interview afterward, called Stevens' remarks "one of the most painful interviews I have watched" and said she had been worried about the congresswoman all week.

Associated Press journalist Mike Householder contributed to this report from Ypsilanti, Michigan. Cappelletti reported from Washington.

articles.title: What polls do and don’t tell us about the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Can the polls be trusted? It depends on what you’re trusting them to do.
articles.body:
Can the polls be trusted? It depends on what you're trusting them to do.

Even the most carefully conducted polls are imprecise snapshots of public opinion, not precision instruments — and when they're pressed into predictive tools, they don't always get it right. But while surveys can't provide an unambiguous answer on who's ahead in tight races, they often do paint a clear and important picture of the political landscape.

The contours of some findings are sharply drawn enough to be visible even through the shadows of potential polling error. Poll after poll has found President Donald Trump's approval rating in the mid-to-low-30s nationally. Surveys also show a broad consensus that Americans, shaken by cost of living concerns , largely take a dim view of the economy and Trump's stewardship of it; that there's little enthusiasm in any corner about the current state of the nation; and that voters are overwhelmingly looking for change — even if they may not all agree on precisely what that change should look like.

Similarly, Democrats' lead on the national " generic ballot " has been consistent and robust enough to suggest that the party has an overall advantage — and it would require an unprecedented level of polling error to overcome that. But there's far less certainty about the precise level of that advantage, or how that might play out in individual races. Even a small difference in Democratic strength compared to what the polls suggest could mean the difference between a blue wave that sweeps well into Republican territory, and one that fails to overcome a deeply Republican-friendly Senate map.

One thing that's challenging for pollsters this year is that there's another finding that looks simultaneously like a defining factor of the race and a potential source of polling error: the yawning gap in partisan enthusiasm about voting.

Polls — consistent with early voting data — have found that, compared to Republicans, Democrats report being far more motivated to vote this year. That's playing a role both in pollsters' efforts to get people to answer surveys, and in their attempts to identify which potential voters will actually end up casting ballots in this election.

Per Gallup , the Democratic enthusiasm advantage is the largest in any midterm dating back to 1994. That's in part because, particularly in his second term, Trump provokes far more fervent opposition than he does ardent support. It also owes in part to the growing education divide in American politics, with college-educated voters likelier than those without degrees both to turn out in a midterm year, and to vote Democratic if they do.

But that same enthusiasm divide could also be shaping voters' willingness to respond to polls.

In a Washington Post-Schar School poll of Kansas, for instance, registered Democrats who were contacted by interviewers were far likelier than registered Republicans to complete the survey. While that disparity hasn't been universal this cycle, the final set of New York Times/Siena College polls also saw a similar response pattern.

This type of variation, sometimes called "differential nonresponse," isn't an entirely new challenge for pollsters. Some types of people have always been more likely than others to answer surveys, including older adults, those with higher levels of education and those who are more civically engaged. Pollsters address that disparity by weighting their results to make the demographics of their sample look more like the broad universe of people they're trying to measure. Increasingly, that also includes weighting to known partisan targets, such as the levels of party registration in a state or vote choice in the 2024 election.

What concerns pollsters are those patterns that aren't fully corrected for, even after weighting to demographic and partisan targets. A poll could have the "right" number of Republicans and Democrats to reflect the electorate but not reach the right mix of voters within each party.

Not every registered voter turns out to cast a ballot in each election — in most years, 40% or more sit it out — and that can also complicate the picture for pollsters. In order to reflect the views of those who do ultimately turn out, pollsters identify likely voters, and those efforts can be complicated by the same factors that make it hard to reach less enthused potential voters.

There's a possibility that some types of Republicans may be too disengaged to respond to surveys, but still sufficiently motivated that they'll end up voting — or that the most engaged and enthusiastic Democrats will be overrepresented in surveys.

Will Republicans sit out or rally for their party?

Even if the polls accurately reflect the dynamics at the time they were conducted, there's still room for a shift after that polling is completed if Republican voters coalesce late around their candidates.

CNN's final state polls , for instance, gave voters an option to say they wouldn't support either candidate in the upcoming Senate race — and even after being asked a follow-up question about which way they'd lean, 6% to 8% in each poll said that, between the two leading candidates, they'd back "neither" or someone else. The poll also pressed voters to choose which party they'd rather see in control of the Senate, even if they initially said it didn't matter to them. Looking at those two questions together tells us that in most of these polls, voters who favor GOP control were more likely than those who'd rather see a Democratic win to opt out of picking a major-party candidate — by about 9 points in Texas, 6 points in Kansas and 4 points in Michigan.

That could well reflect what happens on Election Day. The Republican nominees in Texas and Kansas, Ken Paxton and Roger Marshall, face specific image problems that have made it more difficult for them to consolidate their party's support, and it's fully plausible that GOP-inclined voters in those states might end up taking a pass on the race altogether. But it also suggests that Democrats haven't yet sealed the deal . In a set of relatively tight races, that could be enough to significantly tighten margins or change the outcome of some races altogether.

On the other hand, it's not a given that any polling miss would be in favor of the Democrats. Presidential polls in the past three cycles have underestimated Republicans' share of the vote relative to Democrats : by around 3 points in 2016 and 2024, and close to 5 points in 2020.

But there hasn't been a similar pattern in Trump-era midterm elections . Nor is it guaranteed that polling misses would look the same across the many different states in play.

As we wrote in 2024 , polling data is a single, imperfect gauge of people's opinions. But polls of the US, ultimately, are a means of talking to Americans across a wide range of demographics, life experiences and views, on topics that stretch far beyond elections, or even politics. In a deeply fragmented society, and with social media often reflecting an unrepresentative sample of the loudest voices, they're still a valuable tool for understanding the country as a whole.

articles.summary: "You're gonna have a tremendous win," Trump told voters at a rally in Dubuque.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With Iowa's Senate race tightening, both campaigns are making a final sprint across the state Monday to energize voters ahead of Election Day.

Republican Ashley Hinson 's campaign told NewsNation by phone that confidence is growing by the day, despite polling showing Democrat Josh Turek nearly tied in this toss-up Senate race.

The latest Decision Desk HQ polling average shows Hinson at 53% and Turek at 47%, with the race tightening as Election Day approaches.

The Turek campaign is drawing encouragement from the increasingly competitive numbers, while Hinson's team is brushing off concerns about Republican vulnerabilities in the state.

Hinson's campaign told NewsNation they believe voters are more energized than media coverage suggests.

Still, some Iowa Republicans expressed nervousness Sunday outside a Trump rally in Dubuque. While several supporters said they weren't necessarily expecting a blue wave in Iowa, they acknowledged the races are closer than anticipated.

Trump, however, predicted sweeping Republican victories Tuesday.

"If we win as big as I think we're gonna win, they're going to go back into their holes," Trump said Sunday night. "You're gonna have a tremendous win."

The president also dismissed concerns about polling in Iowa, pointing to his own track record in the state. Trump carried Iowa in three consecutive presidential elections, including a roughly 13-point victory in 2024, despite polling that did not fully capture his margin.

articles.title: Record 40% of registered voters cast ballots during early voting in Texas
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – A record 40% of registered voters, 7. 7 million people, voted during early voting in Texas, according to Secretary of State data.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – A record 40% of registered voters, 7.7 million people, voted during early voting in Texas, according to Secretary of State data.

Instead of voting on one day, Election Day, Texans have 13 days to vote, 12 of which are during an early voting period. This year, early voting went from Oct. 19-30.

There are a record 19 million Texans registered to vote this election, according to Secretary of State data.

By comparison, in 2014, 4.7 million people voted, or 34% of registered voters, according to an analysis of election data by the Austin-based Ryan Data & Research firm.

The company doesn't use modeling information, only data from public SOS registration lists and a list of voters reported by each county on each day of early voting, the company says.

"More people voted early this year than all votes cast in 2014, but we also have five million more registered voters on the registration rolls this year than we did 12 years ago. We also were only 400,000 votes away from surpassing the total for 2022 as well," Derek Ryan with Ryan Data explained in an emailed statement to The Center Square.

He also said that on Election Day, "we are going to see a record number of votes cast for a midterm election in Texas."

By comparison, in 2022, 74% of registered voters voted early. In 2018, the ratio was 80%. In 2024, it was 85%, he said. The ratios were larger in these elections but there were fewer registered voters and the total numbers were less.

The majority of Texans who voted early are in

Harris County saw the highest number of early voters at more than one million, according to SOS data. The county is seen as a bellwether for political shifts in the state. Previously a Republican majority county, over the past 10 years it's shifted left. The majority of voters polled say the state and country are heading in the wrong direction, The Center Square reported. Democrats are expected to make large gains this election despite Gov. Greg Abbott vowing to help turn the county "dark red."

The next largest number of early votes were cast in the state's largest counties: Dallas, Tarrant, Bexar and Travis, according to SOS data. Tarrant County, the state's last large county with a Republican majority, could flip blue on Election Day.

Nearly half of all registered voters in Collin County voted early, according to the data. The county is home to Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who iwho trails in polling in the U.S. Senate race.

The majority of people who voted early were women, 55%, compared to 42% of men.

"Women having an advantage over men isn't out of the ordinary in Texas. There are almost one million more women registered than men. At the completion of early voting in 2018, women made up 54% of all votes cast," Ryan notes.

Nearly 60% of voters over age 65 voted early, according to the data with nearly 2.5 million votes cast, or 32% of early votes cast. "This is a larger share than they had in 2024 after early voting (29%), but smaller than their share in 2022," the analysis notes.

Voters between the ages of 18 and 29 made up nearly one million of the votes, or 13%.

Hispanic voters accounted for nearly 20% of early voters, nearly 1.5 million.

When comparing early voting data to primary voter data, there are 2.7 million people who have not voted who are among the most likely voters, according to the analysis. In this category, Republicans have a 289,717-vote advantage over Democrats if they vote on Election Day, according to Ryan's analysis.

Early voting was not without controversy.

The SOS was sued for problems with a new voter registration system, which officials acknowledged created a backlog of 500,000 registration applications not reaching county registrars. The issue was reportedly fixed ahead of early voting, The Center Square reported. This case is ongoing.

In Harris County, several convicted felons were arrested over the weekend on charges of illegally voting, and last week county officials were sued for running "get out the vote" ads targeting voters by race. The Office of Attorney General investigated both cases. County officials agreed to stop running the ads and were blocked from running them again in the future, The Center Square reported.

In south Texas, an independent investigation found there were 3,500 defective voter registrations in south Texas. The region is where allegations of voter fraud have been made in Zapata County during the Democratic primary elections this year and in 2024, The Center Square reported. County officials who are currently under criminal investigation for alleged voter fraud are running for reelection Nov. 3.
