articles.title: Vance's campaign blitz puts him at the forefront of the GOP's midterm push, as insiders praise packed schedule
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance has held 19 rallies since September as GOP strategists say his midterm election blitz offers a preview of a potential 2028 run.
articles.body: SWANTON, Ohio — As Republicans rally ahead of a midterm election that will determine whether the GOP maintains control of both chambers of Congress, Vice President JD Vance is taking to the campaign trail once again to speak with voters in New York and Ohio on Monday. Vance’s role in the midterm blitz has been eyed by many top GOP strategists and insiders who say his actions on the trail could offer insight into what a 2028 run might look like for the 42-year-old vice president. "Vice President Vance is constantly on the road," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told Fox News Digital. "I believe he's been in just shy of 50 battleground districts and or states this cycle. He's been a workhorse. I mean you look at Donald J. Trump, who's out there constantly. He just doesn't stop. And of course, people don't maybe notice than the vice president is keeping a schedule himself that is frankly incredibly impressive." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE VANCE'S INTIMATE CAPITOL HILL HUDDLE AS REPUBLICANS CONFRONT TOUGH MIDTERM TERRAIN Vance has held 19 rallies since the GOP midterm convention in early September and dozens of events across the country prior to the convention in Dallas. His role in the midterm has fueled further speculation about his potential run for president in 2028. Former White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer explained that his midterm campaign efforts add to his resume, but that his fundraising abilities and his role as finance chair of the Republican National Committee will also be an important advantage that Vance would have in a run for president. SECOND LADY USHA VANCE KEEPS 'OPEN MIND' AMID JD VANCE 2028 SPECULATION "I think which makes this vice president unique, though, is that it's a combination of the policy chops that you just mentioned, but the political chops," Spicer told Fox News Digital I've noted this over and over again that, like, he is the first vice president to ever be the finance chair of the RNC." "His network of donors is going to be a massive advantage if he runs in '28," he added. TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 Vance has repeatedly told reporters that he is focused on his current portfolio of work and has shied away from questions concerning a potential run for the Oval Office. He is, however, the favorite in several prediction markets. President Donald Trump told reporters in late October that he is focused on the midterms before looking at which Republican may run in 2028, saying: "It’s early. We are very early right now. We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes." As for the work Vance is doing off the campaign trail, former White House Chief of Staff and former RNC Chairman Reince Priebus compared the responsibilities of former Vice President Kamala Harris to Vance, saying that Vance has had to take charge of more key issues — from leading the anti-fraud task force to negotiating a peace deal in the Middle East. "If you compare it to the portfolio of Kamala Harris, whose first job was to secure the border, it ended up being a complete and total disaster," Priebus told Fox News Digital. "He's a trusted administrator of huge problems facing our country. So that is very clear. He's a little bit of a whiz kid too." POLL FLASHES WARNING SIGNS FOR REPUBLICANS IN 7 BATTLEGROUND SENATE RACES Pollsters predict that Democrats have an edge in the House as the midterms approach, while the Senate remains "on a knife edge," according to Priebus. The former RNC chairman noted that traditional red and blue waves are far rarer now that in previous midterm elections, noting a smaller number House seats shift between parties every cycle. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND "There are so few districts in our entire country that are up for grabs," Priebus said. "At 435 house seats, how many are really in play? Maybe 30? And in those 30, there's probably only about 5,000 votes in each of those 30 that could go either way. So, that's why you have ripples, I think, nowadays and not waves. The Senate races are all on a knife edge." While President Trump is known for hosting a staggering number of rallies, Vance’s increased presence in the midterm blitz has led to his name emerging alongside President Donald Trump as the face of the party, according to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows. "I think a lot of people have seen him in the shadows of Donald Trump, not as an individual campaigner," Meadows told Fox News Digital. "But as someone who would continue the Trump legacy." THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA "I think for the first time, a broader spectrum of people are seeing JD Vance as the campaigner, and not as a campaigner for him personally," Meadows said. "And, you know, I point out that most of his dynamic interactions have not been in Iowa or New Hampshire or South Carolina." GOP members of Congress have also noted the increased presence of the vice president as they fight to maintain the majority in the House. Rep. Brandon Gill, R-TX, told Fox News Digital he traveled with Vance to Texas and noted the impact that the vice president had in the state. "Kamala Harris couldn't go out and campaign for people because nobody would want to see her," Gill said. "The American people love Vice President Vance. I mean, at all the rallies I've been out with them, they were packed, people were fired up." The vice president held two rallies ahead of the midterm on Monday, one in Rome, New York and the other in Swanton, Ohio – advocating for GOP congressional candidates and pushing for the Republicans to maintain the majority. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Take your friends, take your neighbors, take your grandparents. Get out there and let them know that we are going to send a message that America belongs to those who love it, not those who hate it," Vance told voters in New York on Monday.

articles.title: Mike Rogers dishes on how shock Haley Stevens endorsement unfolded hours before Election Day
articles.summary: GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers defended Dem Rep Haley Stevens as top Democrats erupted over her decision to cross party lines and endorse him over Abdul El...
articles.body:
Michigan Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers praised Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens for putting America ahead of her party Monday while accusing Democrats of viciously attacking the congresswoman after she stunned her party by endorsing him over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed .

Rogers told Brian Kilmeade on the "Brian Kilmeade Show" that Stevens' endorsement "flipped this thing upside down," saying the congresswoman called him Sunday morning while he was on his way to church before ultimately deciding to publicly back his campaign following her bruising primary loss to El-Sayed.

"This is a congresswoman who just stood up and said, 'America is more important than my party right now,'" Rogers said. "And we cannot elect somebody who is so anti-Jewish, who is divisive, who's angry, who was mean about his politics. It's just the wrong thing to do."

Rogers' comments came as Fox News reported Monday that Stevens' endorsement triggered backlash from top Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif.

Schumer called the move a "despicable betrayal," while Pelosi accused Stevens of "dangerously" betraying Michigan families by backing Rogers.

The endorsement marked a dramatic break for Stevens, who had stopped short of explicitly endorsing El-Sayed in the weeks after losing the Democratic primary but continued to publicly align herself with the party. During an October CNN interview, Stevens was repeatedly pressed on whether she supported El-Sayed and declined to explicitly say she endorsed him, instead stressing that she was "still on the team" and planned to support Democrats on the ballot.

The tensions between the former primary rivals had been building in the closing stretch of the race. Stevens pressed El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices, which she called antisemitic, before El-Sayed's campaign asked her to stay away from its remaining campaign events. El-Sayed said his campaign did not produce the ad and that he disagreed with its contents.

Meanwhile, days before she publicly endorsed Rogers, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, had already broken with the Democratic nominee. Turkish, a Jewish Michigan attorney and registered Democrat, told reporters at a Rogers campaign event that he planned to vote for the Republican, arguing that El-Sayed's rhetoric on Israel had made the Jewish community "less safe." Turkish described his decision as "putting country before party."

Still, even hours before the endorsement, Stevens appeared to be denying that she planned to back Rogers. Fox News Digital reported Monday that Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said she spoke with Stevens around midnight Saturday and was told reports of an impending Rogers endorsement were a "rumor" and "not true."

However, hours later, Stevens was standing alongside Rogers at a Detroit church service, where she ultimately announced she would cross party lines and endorse him over El-Sayed.

"We didn't know what was going to happen. We were driving to the church yesterday morning when the call came in," Rogers said. "I just invited her to come in. She decided between when she got in the car and she got to the church, she was going to not only withdraw the endorsement, but endorse me."

Rogers, who said the pair had a "great conversation" on the phone, also pushed back on suggestions that Stevens had received anything in exchange for the endorsement, saying his campaign had no advance knowledge that she planned to back him.

"Absolutely not. Matter of fact, we didn't know what was going to happen," Rogers said when asked whether he had offered Stevens anything. "She said, 'I've not asked anyone to go with me, I'm just telling you what I'm doing.'"

Rogers then took aim at Democrats who have attacked Stevens since her announcement.

"They want to attack Haley Stevens for saying, 'I'm a Democrat, I'm voting Democrat up and down the ticket, except for one race, Abdul El-Sayed. I am voting for Mike Rogers,'" Rogers said.

"Their whole plan now is to come out and attack her with viciousness," he continued. "She's the only one in the Democrat Party today that has enough common sense to know you elect somebody that hates a group of people this much, it's gonna be a disaster for Democrats and America."

During his appearance on Kilmeade's radio show, Rogers was pressed on a New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday that showed El-Sayed leading him 53% to 42% among likely Michigan voters, a significantly wider margin than other surveys of the race.

Rogers rejected the findings, pointing to his campaign's internal polling and modeling, which he said showed the race within one or two points.

"We have it as a one- or two-point race," Rogers said. "Our polling, our modeling and polling shows this is tied or we're up by two. So we think that's closer to the truth."

Rogers also argued that the poll underestimated his support among Black voters in Detroit , saying his campaign had made "great inroads" in the community.

His comments come after Stevens publicly questioned El-Sayed's outreach to Black voters. During the October CNN interview, when she would not explicitly back El-Sayed, Stevens said she had urged El-Sayed and his campaign to deliver a speech to the Black community.

"But yeah, I mean, that didn't happen," Stevens said at the time. "That speech hasn't happened."

articles.title: DOJ appeals to Supreme Court to set aside 20,000 California ballots from suspected noncitizens. Here's what to know.
articles.summary: The Justice Department says more than 20,000 people it suspects may be noncitizens were mailed ballots. A federal appeals court twice rejected the request, w...
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday appealed to the Supreme Court to order California election officials to set aside mail-in ballots from people it believes are noncitizens.

The administration's latest move comes after a federal appeals court twice rejected the Department of Justice's request to stop California from processing the ballots of 20,000 people it suspects may be noncitizens.

The Trump administration has said the ballots should not be counted until the voters' citizenship statuses can be verified, according to the Associated Press . Election officials say the list is unreliable and likely includes many citizens' names. A district judge last week warned that setting aside the ballots could disenfranchise citizens.

What is the Justice Department asking for?

The department wants counties to "segregate — not cancel" the mail-in ballots of people on its list until their citizenship can be confirmed, according to a letter to San Bernardino County obtained by NBC News last month. That county's list included 1,133 names.

It also asked counties to send identifying information about the voters on the list, including Social Security numbers and copies of their registrations, the AP reported .

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, who signed the letters.

Why does the administration say it's necessary?

The Department of Homeland Security compared California's voter registration files with federal immigration records. It flagged more than 20,000 people it says are "likely" noncitizens who are registered to vote, according to a Justice Department release . Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot.

Voting throughout the state began in early October, and hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. In its appeal to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration asked for a "limited injunction" to set aside the ballots while the case plays out.

"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, according to the AP .

Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal and state elections. "Even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the release.

Essayli says the request is limited. "We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," he told Fox News last month.

State officials say the federal data hasn't been verified, and that acting on it could keep eligible citizens from voting. In court filings, lawyers for the state argued that counties lack both the authority and the federal records needed to check citizenship. They also said the demand could delay certification of the results.

Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County clerk, said a letter that the DOJ sent demanding help identifying noncitizens carried "a posture of intimidation and threats" just before the election, CNN reported . Sen. Alex Padilla, a Democrat of California, said the administration "has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud."

On Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law."

Last week, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who ruled against the federal government's request, suggested that setting aside the ballots could "wreak havoc" on the election.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," he wrote. "This Court declines to be a party to such process."

Cases do happen, but reviews have found very few. In 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, audited the state's voter rolls and found 20 noncitizens among about 8.2 million registered voters.

Federal claims have not always held up. In August, DHS told Nevada officials it had flagged about 15,900 possible noncitizen registrants. It later said that number was preliminary and that it had confirmed only 185 through manual review, CNN reported . In September, Nevada officials said their own review found that all 185 were U.S. citizens. DHS disputes that finding.

What does this mean for California voters?

For now, nothing has changed. No court has ordered California to set aside any ballots, and counties are still processing the ballots voters return. Voters can check the status of their ballot through the secretary of state's ballot tracking tool .

articles.title: Pentagon's top spies tasked with 'no-fail' mission as Hegseth puts foreign midterm meddling in crosshairs
articles.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's September directive mobilizes the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise for midterm election security overseas.
articles.body:
Ever since the 2016 presidential election that first got President Donald Trump elected and the ensuing Russiagate scandal, there has been increased scrutiny on foreign meddling in U.S. elections and threats to the American voting system.

Now, 10 years later, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is directing his entire intelligence and spy forces to ensure foreign adversaries do not interfere in Tuesday's midterms.

The Pentagon chief has ordered America's military intelligence and cyber agencies to mobilize against foreign threats to the 2026 elections by directing his department's sprawling intelligence apparatus to make election security a priority in what he calls a "no-fail mission."

The September directive reaches beyond U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency , instructing the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise — including agencies responsible for military and geospatial intelligence — to "mobilize every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" against foreign election threats.

The order puts some of the military's most sophisticated intelligence capabilities behind a mission that has grown considerably since Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election. But with Americans preparing to vote, the extent to which Hegseth's directive has changed the Pentagon's existing election-security operations remains unclear.

The Department of War declined to provide Fox News Digital with additional details about how the order is being implemented. Cyber Command separately declined an interview request about its election-security efforts.

In practice, the directive can mean military intelligence agencies are tasked with identifying foreign hackers or influence operations overseas, warning civilian agencies about threats headed toward U.S. targets and, when authorized, Cyber Command taking action against the foreign actors or infrastructure behind them.

The military's role largely stops at the U.S. border: state and local officials run elections, while agencies such as the FBI and Department of Homeland Security handle the domestic side.

The Pentagon's election security mission is not new. Cyber Command and NSA have spent years tracking and disrupting foreign threats around American elections, including operations targeting Russian actors during previous election cycles.

The effort began taking its current shape ahead of the 2018 midterms, when the agencies formed a "Russia Small Group" focused on foreign interference. It later evolved into a joint Election Security Group, combining NSA's intelligence-gathering capabilities with Cyber Command's ability to conduct operations against foreign cyber threats.

By 2022, then-Cyber Command and NSA chief Gen. Paul Nakasone was describing election security as an "enduring, no-fail mission" — language echoed by Hegseth four years later.

"Rest assured, we were doing operations well before the midterms began, and we were doing operations likely on the day of the midterms," Nakasone said after the 2022 election, describing the military's role as "understanding your foreign adversaries and operating outside the United States."

The agencies again established an Election Security Group for the 2024 presidential election, but whether that structure was recreated for this year's midterms has been less clear.

Gen. Joshua Rudd, the current head of Cyber Command and NSA, told lawmakers in April that foreign interference was "reasonable to expect based on what we've seen in the past" and said his command was "postured and ready to support as required or tasked." He said at the time that he was unsure whether the Election Security Group had been reconvened.

Five months later, Hegseth issued his department-wide directive, addressed not only to Cyber Command and NSA but also to the directors of the Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The order instructs military intelligence agencies to collect and analyze intelligence on foreign election threats while directing Cyber Command to use its existing authorities and capabilities to counter potential foreign cyber activity in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security .

It does not publicly grant new authorities or establish a new election-security organization, instead reinforcing a mission the military has increasingly treated as an enduring responsibility.

U.S. intelligence officials, meanwhile, say they have seen no evidence that a foreign adversary has attempted to interfere with voting machines, physical election infrastructure or the counting of votes ahead of Tuesday's midterms.

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said last week that intelligence officials continue to see nothing contradicting that assessment, but urged Americans to remain "on high alert" for foreign disinformation , particularly as artificial intelligence makes such campaigns easier to spread.

But officials continue to track foreign influence efforts from Russia, China and Iran, with Russia remaining the most active foreign influence threat, CNN reported Sunday.

U.S. elections are attractive targets for foreign adversaries because the stakes extend far beyond who wins office: influencing American voters or undermining confidence in the process can shape U.S. policy, weaken public support for policies they oppose and deepen divisions without ever touching a voting machine.

Lawmakers briefed on classified intelligence last month said Russia was using disinformation to target candidates and undermine confidence in the election, while China's influence efforts were more narrowly focused on candidates viewed as hostile to Beijing.

The Pentagon's role focuses on threats originating overseas, while state and local officials administer elections and civilian federal agencies lead domestic election-security efforts.

Hegseth's directive makes that overseas mission a priority across the broader military intelligence enterprise, though the Pentagon has not disclosed whether it has resulted in additional personnel, resources or organizational changes ahead of Election Day.

articles.title: Ahead of Election Day, Trump sets the stage for potential Republican losses
articles.summary: President Donald Trump acknowledged historical trends against the president’s party in midterm elections, saying Monday, “We gave this a very strong shot.”
articles.body:
In an election-eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot" while acknowledging that historically, the president's party "doesn't win the midterms."

"This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime," Trump said Monday in his final major speech before the midterm elections Tuesday. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up."

Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump's "closing message" before voters make their final trips to the polls, Trump spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool.

Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, a key focus and fascination of his second term.

Speaking about the election, he touted what he considered economic wins, saying that "personal incomes are the highest in history" and that "the poverty rate is at an all-time record low."

But, he said, "it all doesn't matter if we're going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election."

"If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election ... just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide," he continued. "Now, that doesn't happen, because usually, whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad — for some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot."

Trump derided Democratic candidates and falsely said some were jihadists or members of the Muslim Brotherhood. He said they are "all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy costs skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world, hoping to get them to be able to vote."

Trump referred to Alaska's Senate race and last week's report by The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent. Peltola has denied having been aware of the reported scheme.

"They got somebody named Dan Sullivan to run against Dan Sullivan," Trump said. "It's corrupt. It's really a fraud, fraudulent election."

Asked by NBC News after his remarks whether he would consider resuming strikes on Iran after the election, Trump said, "No."

Trump closed out a 28-rally swing through the U.S. to campaign for Republican candidates Sunday. He traveled for 25 days in the final month of the campaign, visiting 19 states. He held his final rallies outside Washington on Sunday, with one in Kansas and the other in Iowa, both states with competitive Senate races.

Trump is scheduled to participate in several tele-rallies for the midterms from Washington on Monday. On the final day of the 2018 midterm election cycle, by contrast, he held in-person rallies in three states.

"We've got some big races tomorrow," Trump said in his remarks. "I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow's Election Day, more traditional."

Asked Sunday why he chose to speak at the Reflecting Pool, Trump told reporters: "Just to show how beautiful it is. It's been finished. It was vandalized badly. We have cameras all over the place now for the vandals."

On Monday, he stood next to a poster that said, "Back, and more beautiful than ever."

"We're booming like we've never boomed before," he said. "We've cleaned hundreds of sites of graffiti, fixed over 2,300 lighting fixtures in Washington, D.C., cleaned and renovated over 83 statues and fountains and monuments, removed hundreds of squalid homeless encampments."

In addition to the Reflecting Pool between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II Memorial downtown, Trump highlighted other construction projects he launched, including the White House ballroom , a White House helipad , a new golf course in the city and a triumphal arch , among other projects.

Trump appeared to joke at one point that the Reflecting Pool would be named after him.

The Reflecting Pool has been closed since July after additional renovations had to be made when the bottom coating peeled and algae formed, tinting the water green.

The National Park Service announced recently that it was extending the closure of the pool and the areas surrounding it until Nov. 20.

After the initial renovation process began in June and it first reopened to the public, Trump accused multiple people of "destroying" the pool.

The U.S. attorney's office in Washington charged former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with destruction of property during a June 19 visit. In late July, the U.S. attorney's office, led by Jeanine Pirro, dropped the case , citing information it had obtained that undermined "the evidentiary basis for the indictment."

articles.title: What early voting does and doesn’t tell us about the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Approximately 54 million Americans have offered a glimpse into the midterm election, which is seeing an uptick in younger and racially diverse voters.
articles.body:
On the eve of Election Day a record number of Americans have already passed judgement on President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress.

Roughly 54 million voters cast their early ballots over this past weekend ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab .

The deluge offers a glimpse into a forecasted wave election that many experts believe could sweep Democrats in power for the president's final two years in the White House.

Every state has different rules on compiling voters' age, race or party affiliation with some providing no demographic statistics at all. But it does reveal important voter behavior and some demographics that paint a clearer picture about who is more motivated in the 2026 midterms.

‘I voted’ stickers show unique election pride at midterm polls

Michael McDonald, a political science professor who runs the Election Lab, said the initial outlook indicates a younger, more diverse and politically independent electorate is showing up.

"I can confidently say that the 2026 election will be the most diverse midterm electorate in U.S. history," in an Oct. 28 post on X.

But the data alone, much like the various polls , cannot predict the outcome of who will be in charge of the House and Senate next year, McDonald and others have warned.

Here's a look at the big takeaways from the early voting totals.

A lot more people are showing up than in 2022

For starters, 8 million more people took advantage of the early in-person and mail-in ballot options over the weekend than during the last 2022 midterms, which gave Republicans control of the House during former President Joe Biden 's term.

Political observers are marveling at those numbers and note how they surged in places with more competitive Senate contests, such as Ohio, Maine and Michigan.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton have locked horns in arguably the most watched race of this year's cycle. The early totals show more than 7.7 million people have cast early ballots, which surpasses the Lone Star State's high mark of 40% turnout during the 2018 midterms.

"Their record for a midterm election is 8.3 million total. So they're just over about 600,000 or so ballots away from their highest turnout ever... Election Day hasn't even happened yet. That's remarkable," David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said during CBS' Face the Nation on Nov. 1.

Progressive left and socialist candidates shaping the 2026 midterms

Democrats saw a burst of momentum following the successful campaign of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani . From grassroots movements to national races, here are the progressive candidates running in 2026 midterms . Abdul El-Sayed is a former Detroit-based public health official who is Michigan's Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate. He is a progressive, defeating the more moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the primary, but El-Sayed has said he is not a democratic socialist.

Same goes for Georgia, where more than 2.8 million voters have showed up already representing a 13% increase compared to 2022; Michigan with more than 2.3 million marking a 26% increase; and South Carolina where about 1.1 million have shown up compared to approximately 620,000 four years ago which is a whomping 75% increase.

Records were also broken in North Carolina, where Democrats are hoping former Gov. Roy Cooper can flip a GOP-held Senate seat against former RNC Chair Michael Whatley. The Tar Heel State began sending out early voting mail-in ballots Oct. 15 and combined with in-person about 2.8 million have reportedly showed up already.

That is a 31% increase compared to the midterm election four years ago, Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper said in an Oct. 31 post on Substack .

"Voter turnout was higher on every day of early voting than on the comparable day in 2022," he said.

'Bloodbath': Democrats, independents turnout is up while GOP is down

Far more Democrats than Republicans made their voices heard in the early voting process with some states outpacing their 2024 presidential totals, the preliminary data show.

Of the 54 million ballots cast, about 43% were from Democrats and 32% were from GOP voters, with the about 25% coming from independent or "unaffiliated" voters.

Keep in mind that these statistics are limited to the 27 states that report party affiliation. It also reflects the voter's registration rather than their exact choice on the ballot.

But some Republicans are already expressing nervousness about the low GOP turnout , especially given Trump's unpopularity among those showing up more. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 8, for example, found 25% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the economy, with just 9% of Democrats and 23% of independents agreeing.

"I am deeply, deeply worried. What we're seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout," Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, during an Oct. 30 episode of "The Verdict," his podcast.

"Democrats are showing up. They are energized. They hate, hate, hate Donald Trump. If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far were counted, Republicans would lose massively. It would not be close. We would lose both the House and Senate. It would be a bloodbath."

Trump rallies supporters in Chillicothe, Ohio ahead of midterms

For the past several weeks Trump and his allies have been zig-zagging across the nation, focusing heavily on conservative strongholds in order to motivate their base. He is set to speak at the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., capping off a blitz of last-minute appearances in states where Republicans face competitive challengers.

GOP voters historically have swarmed Election Day when tens of millions of Americans will likely to flock the polls as well, but experts say the early voting patterns mirror past trends.

"It would be highly unusual for Election Day to be dramatically different than in the past, so I would not hold out hope for a huge Republican wave to make up for their in-person early voting deficit where we are seeing a lack of Republican early voting engagement," McDonald said on his Substack.

Racially diverse and younger voters fueling turnout

The United States is becoming a more racially and ethnically diverse nation, and that's showing up in our elections as a higher percentage of Black and Hispanic voters make up the electorate.

Of the handful of states that submit race and ethnicity information from early voting totals there is a noteworthy uptick among voters of color, while voting among White people lags behind and remains similar to 2022 levels.

Hispanic turnout in Texas is especially noteworthy given it has exceeded the 2024 presidential levels , fueled largely by younger voters, Tom Bonier, a Democratic data and polling expert, told USA TODAY in an October interview. In the state's predominantly Hispanic counties, analysts say they are finding turnout to be higher than the statewide average.

Trump and the GOP will need to hold their gains among Hispanic voters , who helped fuel his 2024 victory but has soured on the administration especially over its strict immigration enforcement campaign.

The Pew Research Center found Trump's approval among Hispanic voters sits at 24% , which is down from 38% in February 2025.

Among Black voters, who make up a larger share of the South electorate, there is reported anger of Trump's redistricting war that carved up many majority-Black congressional districts. That is could help to fuel a surge being seen in southern states such as Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, where there's a Senate race surprisingly within the margin of error .

The Election Lab shows Black early voting accounts for about 32% of Georgia's turnout thus far, which is about three percentage points better than during the 2022 midterm.

Even that small jump, however, can be significant given the Peach State's toss-up status, particularly in its closely watched race for governor between Democrat Keisha Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, and Republican Keith Jackson, a healthcare CEO.

In South Carolina, for instance, the numbers show Black voters making up about 27% of the electorate which is significantly higher than in past cycles overall.

McDonald said by all indicators this midterm should be a good one for Democrats and that figures coming from these states show elevated engagement from those demographics.

"Since the Democratic coalition is more diverse, their higher engagement levels will yield a more diverse electorate," he said.

articles.title: Illinois Quick Hits: Voters consider candidates, tax and spend measures on Election Day
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Polls are scheduled to be open from 6 a. m.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Polls are scheduled to be open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. across Illinois on Election Day.

Voters have the opportunity to select the state's next U.S. senator, as well as members of Congress, governor and other statewide offices, members of the state legislature and more.

More than 50 tax and borrowing measures are on the ballot in local jurisdictions across Illinois. Sales tax referendums are up for consideration in Adams, Lake and Tazewell counties.

According to the Illinois State Board of Elections, electioneering is prohibited within 100 horizontal feet of a polling place. Churches, places of worship and private schools may designate their entire property as a campaign-free zone.

One killed, three hurt at football game shooting in Madison

Investigators are asking for tips after a shooting at a youth football league championship game in Madison, Illinois on Sunday night left one person dead and four injured.

According to a statement from the Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis, the incident happened around 9:49 p.m. at Madison Senior High School. One adult was pronounced dead at the scene, and three other adults were reported in stable condition at area hospitals.

U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft said federal resources have been directed to assist the Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis and the Madison Police Department.

An FBI tip line was created to receive photos and videos from the incident, but the public's help is needed to identify people involved. Photos and videos can be uploaded online .

Authorities identify teen killed in Bloomington mass shooting

McLean County authorities have identified the teen killed in a shooting that left seven others injured in Bloomington early Sunday.

Police said on Monday that Giana Detloff, 19, of Carol Stream was visiting one of her best friends when the shooting occurred at a house in the 100 block of East Division Street.

Detloff was a student and cheerleader at North Central College in Naperville following her graduation from Glenbard North High School last spring. As of Monday afternoon, no arrests had been made in connection with the shooting.

The Bloomington Police Department provided a Community Portal for potential evidence related to the incident.

articles.body:
Several states are expecting close races on Election Day , which will determine who will run Congress during President Donald Trump 's final two years in office.

Perhaps one of the largest polling leads among the battleground states is in Michigan , where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers are going head to head .

On Nov. 1, Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed, announced in a social media video that she endorses Rogers . The decision surprised friends and party leaders, with some Democrats sharing that Stevens, as recently as Oct. 31, said she planned to support El-Sayed.

"This is just a weight off my shoulders, okay? Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier," Stevens told CNN's Anderson Cooper on Nov. 1. "I'm making a decision here, and that's just where I landed on this. I woke up this morning, clear-eyed, fresh, and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."

Days before, El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to not attend any of his campaign events , as previously reported by USA TODAY.

With Election Day tomorrow, here's what to know about El-Sayed and Rogers' standings.

Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed clash in fiery final debate of campaign

Who is leading the polls for Michigan Senate?

As of Nov. 2, El-Sayed was, on average, leading the polls by five points, according to political poll tracker FiftyPlusOne , which compiled data from organizations like The New York Times and YouGov . Here's a closer look at those numbers:

articles.title: Trump promised 35 midterm stops, but fell short. Here's where he went
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he would travel to 35 places with competitive midterm races. Instead, he went to a handful of states that backed him. See where.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has been on the campaign trail night after night for the last several weeks in hopes of a Republican victory in the midterms.

Trump laid out his plans at a Rose Garden dinner on Sept. 2 , rallying House Republicans to defy the historical trend that sees the president's party lose ground in the midterms.

"I'm gonna take the final 30 days, maybe a little bit more than that, because it's all about 35 races," Trump said. "I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places, and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected."

Trump did not make it to 35 places, though the blitz was still jam-packed. Today, Trump capped it off with remarks in Washington, D.C., at the site of ongoing controversy: the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Here is where Trump did go on his midterm blitz:

Inside President Donald Trump's red state midterm blitz — Photos

Since Trump announced his midterm blitz in September, he has traveled to 31 places for different political rallies, including Dallas for the Republican midterm convention, according to an analysis of his public schedule compiled by Factbase .

The stops were concentrated on a handful of states, many of which Trump won easily in his presidential races. Here is the rundown:

Texas - 4 rallies and the Republican midterm convention ( Denton , San Antonio , Lubbock and Corpus Christi )

Ohio - 3 rallies ( Vandalia , Youngstown and Chillicothe )

Florida - 2 rallies ( Fort Myers and Daytona Beach )

Kansas - 2 rallies ( Park City and Salina )

South Carolina - 2 rallies ( Pendleton and Rock Hill )

North Carolina - 2 rallies ( Gastonia and Greenville )

Georgia - 2 rallies ( Dalton and Perry )

Iowa - 2 rallies ( Sioux City and Dubuque )

Of the Senate races rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, Maine is the only place he did not go, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is trying to keep her seat in a state that he lost in 2024. He has also called into telerallies for candidates in Virginia, Pennsylvania and more.

"Nobody works harder than President Trump ," said White House spokesperson Liz Huston in response to questions about what states he didn't make it to. "President Trump has been on the road nonstop, traveling across the country to highlight what his administration has delivered for the American people."

The president is scheduled to be at the White House on election night. He already cast his vote in Palm Beach County, Florida .

articles.title: US midterms campaign set to be most expensive ever recorded
articles.summary: The 2026 campaign is projected to cost nearly $12bn - BBC Verify looks into where all that money has come from.
articles.body:
The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.

Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.

The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.

BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.

There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.

But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.

According to the latest Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.

Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.

Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.

However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.

This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.

The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice , which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.

"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.

As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.

Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.

Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.

But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.

Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.

America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.

"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.

Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.

However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.

In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact .

"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.

Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.

articles.title: Reflecting Pool dominates Trump’s closing midterm speech
articles.summary: President Trump’s closing speech a day before the midterm elections focused on the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other changes around...
articles.body:
President Trump's closing speech a day before the midterm elections focused on the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other changes around Washington, D.C.

Trump in remarks at the Reflecting Pool announced its reopening. He showed pictures of what was replaced and said it should be a project that "unites all Americans."

"Today, I'm thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool," he said.

He said they were considering renaming it the Trump Reflecting Pool but then said he was joking.

The pool has been fenced off for months after algae blooms and slits in the lining plagued the original renovation that Trump wanted.

The president didn't touch on the midterm elections until roughly 20 minutes into his speech, focusing mostly on the pool repairs and other efforts to beautify D.C. , such as fixing fountains, removing graffiti and cutting down on crime.

"As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up."

He touted his administration's achievements and hit on several candidates, such as Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, repeating claims about the nominee's ties to the Muslim Brotherhood . Trump also touched on Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who is running against incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

"We've achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I've kept every single promise I made, except far more," he said. "I've actually kept far more promises than I made. We've done much more than I promised, and we have the most secure border in American history."

He repeated his promise of giving American adults a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterms.

He noted that he has traveled extensively the last few weeks to hold rallies, saying they were "full of love."

"America is ready to go," he said. "They're ready to vote. I hope they're ready to do the right thing."

Trump said Republicans gave this election cycle "a very strong shot."

"For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot," he said.

Trump spoke briefly about not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon before bringing his speech back to the Reflecting Pool.

articles.title: Battleground Dem touts bipartisan record, but can’t name single issue she’d work with Trump on
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan touted her bipartisan record but couldn't name one Trump policy she'd support, citing "continued grift."
articles.body: A Democratic Senate candidate in Minnesota touted her bipartisan record Sunday but could not name a single issue she would work with President Donald Trump on, instead accusing his administration of "continued grift." The exchange came as Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s Democratic Senate nominee, campaigns against Republican Michele Tafoya in a race Republicans see as a rare opportunity to flip a traditionally blue state. Flanagan’s answer underscored the sharply partisan nature of the Minnesota race, where she has cast Tafoya as a rubber stamp for Trump and pledged to oppose the administration at nearly every turn. "I just want to be really clear that I’ve got a long track record of working with folks on the other side of the aisle," Flanagan told Fox News' Bill Melugin when asked if there were any policies she could see herself working with Trump on. Flanagan pointed to her work at the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and her time in the Minnesota Legislature, where she served alongside a Republican majority and helped pass bipartisan legislation, as evidence of her ability to work across the aisle. "I think that, you know, that proves that I have the ability to work with folks," she continued. PEGGY FLANAGAN DEMANDS EXPANDING THE SUPREME COURT AND ABOLIHING ICE Flanagan’s bipartisan pitch comes against the backdrop of a campaign built around opposing Trump’s agenda. She has called for dismantling ICE, passing Medicare for All, and reversing the administration’s Medicaid and SNAP cuts, while accusing Trump of using the presidency to enrich himself. "Right now, I’m deeply concerned about the Trump administration, the continued grift, making money hand over fist directly from the Oval Office," she continued in her response to Melugin on whether she would work with Trump on anything. The Democratic Senate candidate went on to tell Melugin that what she has been "hearing" on the campaign trail is that voters want someone who will be a "check" on Trump, not his ally. "They’re interested in whether people are going to be a check on this guy, and roll back some of the devastating cuts and impacts on Minnesota," Flanagan concluded in her answer about working with Trump. "That’s the place I’m going to start." Flanagan is facing Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter who has turned the race into a referendum on the massive fraud scandal that unfolded under the Walz administration. Tafoya has argued that Flanagan, who served as Walz’s No. 2 as lieutenant governor, should share responsibility for the scandal, while also tying her opponent to progressive positions, including Medicare for All and dismantling ICE. MN SENATE CANDIDATE RIPPED FOR BLAMING WALZ FOR FRAUD DESPITE BEING HIS #2: 'KNOWS SHE'S COOKED' The race has become unexpectedly competitive after Tafoya narrowed the gap in Minnesota, prompting Fox News to shift its rating from "Likely Democrat" to "Lean Democrat." "The more that Minnesotans learn about me and my opponent and see what my opponent has failed to do over the last eight years alongside [Democratic Gov.] Tim Walz, they're understanding Minnesota needs change. We need fresh ideas, we need an independent thinker and they're jumping on board," Tafoya said in a Fox News Digital interview. Flanagan has repeatedly tied Tafoya to Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in Minnesota. "Michele Tafoya is all in for Donald Trump — and he's all in for her," Flanagan said last month in a social media post. But Tafoya appears to be putting some daylight between herself and Trump, as she highlights her support for abortion rights. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I’m a pro-choice Republican not afraid to stand up to my party," Tafoya says in a new campaign commercial. "When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he is wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota." While the ad drew opposition from some Republicans, including Mercedes Schlapp, a senior fellow at the Conservative Political Action Conference, Trump subsequently signaled support for Tafoya at an Ohio rally he headlined. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person," the president said. Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump spotlights Reflecting Pool repairs in closing midterm message
articles.summary: Trump warned that the Democratic Party had nominated 'the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.'
articles.body:
Standing before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump focused his closing pitch to midterm voters on his controversial Washington, D.C., construction projects, reducing crime in the nation's capital and improvements to the White House.

A day before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump touted the construction of a helipad on the South Lawn, sprucing up Lafayette Park and Columbus Circle, re-grassing the lawn in front of the White House and his plans for a 250-foot Triumphal Arch.

And he delved at length into the Reflecting Pool project itself, which was marked by six months of false starts before finally opening last week, holding up photos for emphasis and speaking for more than 20 minutes before mentioning the midterms.

When he did, he warned that the Democratic Party had nominated "the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history."

Inside President Donald Trump's red state midterm blitz — Photos

With polls and prognosticators showing a Democratic surge in the midterm stretch's final days and voter concern solidly focused on cost of living issues, the president's decision to close out his 28-rally campaign blitz with a speech focused on construction in Washington, D.C., was unexpected.

"And by the way, we resurfaced the granite. This granite was all resurfaced," Trump said, speaking under a cloudy sky over the occasional sound of airplanes flying overhead, with the calm water of the pool behind him, and further in the distance the Washington Monument.

"We've now fixed all the piping, it's in great shape," he later added, also displaying a photo of the "tremendous algae problem" he said plagued the pool.

A sign next to the reflecting pool announced: "Back, and more beautiful than ever!"

The message he aimed to send was clear: He is literally and metaphorically fixing Washington.

"We fought for 250 years to make it great. We're not going let it be torn down by a bunch of people that have failed everywhere they've been because of... various ideologies, they've always failed every single time," said Trump. "So we'll defend our country, our culture and our heritage for generations to come. We're going to keep it the way it."

Whether that sometimes meandering message resonates with voters during a midterm cycle focused on cost of living concerns will be determined on Nov. 3. Trump spent nearly an hour making the case, gathering media and a few guests - including uniformed National Park Service workers - for a more sedate event than the raucous rallies he has staged from Alaska to Florida in recent weeks.

The midterm map has proven difficult for Republicans. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates 222 House districts as favoring Democratic candidates, more than enough to claim the 218-seat majority. Of the 18 "toss-up" districts, 14 are currently represented by Republicans.

On the Senate side, Democrats lead their Republican rivals in six of the seven contested states that will determine control of the Senate and are tied in a seventh, according to a final set of polls before the midterm elections from The New York Times and Siena University . Six of those seven seats are currently held by Republicans.

Trump has beseeched voters to "pretend" he is on the ballot, but he is also battling low approval numbers. His approval rating sits at 37% according to an Emerson College poll , marking a new low ahead of the midterm elections.

The president on Nov. 2, however, sought to highlight accomplishments including bringing crime down, getting rid of homeless encampments and graffiti on the monuments in Washington, D.C.

Among construction projects he's undertaken including demolishing the East Wing to build a ballroom, a 250-foot-tall triumphal arch, repaving the Rose Garden and remaking the the John F. Kennedy Performing Arts Center.

The president put his D.C. renovations efforts at the center of his closing message even as polls show most Americans have concerns about them. A Washington Post-Ipsos survey from July found that 65% of Americans say they are dissatisfied or upset with three Trump priorities: The reflecting pool, ballroom and arch.

Trump also claimed during his speech that the U.S. had won the war with Iran, even as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to commercial traffic, causing fluctuating oil and gas prices and adding to voter anxiety.

"I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon," he said. "We allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon this country could never function the same way."

The reflecting pool saga began in April after the administration awarded two no-bid contracts to repair the pool in preparation for America's 250 th anniversary celebrations on July 4.

Trump first publicly announced the project to transform the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on April 23 during an event at the Oval Office, describing the pool as a "filthy, dirty" place that was " leaking like a sieve. "

Trump said he'd asked a contractor to choose the color "American flag blue" for the bottom of the pool. He estimated the project would cost $1.5 million and said the work would last "30, 40, 50 years."

By the following day, April 24, he adjusted the price to $2 million and said it would be done in "one week" in a Truth Social post.

But an analysis of federal contract data by USA TODAY found that 20 days before Trump first announced the project and its estimated $1.5 million cost, a company named Atlantic Industrial Coatings had already been contracted for nearly $6.9 million to take on the project on April 3. In addition, Green Water Solutions, an Ohio-based company, had been awarded a no-bid contract for over $1.7 million.

In the following weeks, Atlantic Industrial would be paid more: on May 8, it received $6,218,381; the company was given $1,086,576 on June 3.

Trump announced the project was complete on June 6, and the pool was refilled with water during the week of June 8.

Within a few days, algae blooms had turned the water green. Algae has been a recurring problem at the pool for decades. In addition, pieces of the new blue paint had begun peeling up from the bottom.

Trump blamed vandalism for the algae and the peeling paint despite the pool's history of algae problems. Somebody had put fertilizer in the water to create algae, Trump said on June 22. He also said vandals had "very violently" cut a "350-foot slit from one end to the other" in the pool, causing the paint to peel.

The National Park Service began pouring hydrogen peroxide into the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to kill aggressive, recurring algae blooms in the 6.75-million-gallon capacity pool. Despite Trump's claims, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, acknowledged problems with the installation and agreed to complete repairs under its warranty.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a legal filing dismissing charges against an Olympian accused of vandalizing the pool that "the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism."

On Nov. 2, Trump again blamed vandals for the damage to the reflecting pool.

"The vandals went to work, but we also went to work on the vandals," he said.

Trump has described Washington, D.C., as America's front door and has undertaken various construction and renovation projects both in the White House complex and around the capital.

As someone with a background in real estate, working on "fixing things" such as the 90,000 square-foot East Wing Modernization Project which includes the 20,000 square-foot ballroom are projects Trump has said help him "relax."

During the speech, Trump also repeated his promise of $5,000 "Trump Dividend" check to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans maintaining control of both the House and the Senate.

"It's the golden age of America," he said. "We have a country that we can be proud of again."

A few protesters descended on the reflecting pool after the president departed. Maryland resident Nadine Seiler, 61, wore a pink frog costume and carried a banner criticizing Trump for focusing on the reflecting pool.

"What are our priorities here in the United States?" Seiler said. "The price of gas is high. The price of food is high, credit card debt... housing costs, but we care about the reflecting pool?"

S wapna Venugopal Ramaswamy is a White House correspondent for USA TODAY. You can follow her on X @SwapnaVenugopal .

articles.title: Trump approval nears record low before Election Day: poll
articles.summary: Trump’s approval sits near a record low as Republicans trail Democrats with Election Day less than 24 hours away, according to latest Reuters poll.
articles.body:
With Election Day less than 24 hours away, President Donald Trump 's approval rating remains near a record low as Republicans trail Democrats in the race for Congress, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll .

The poll, released Monday, Nov. 2, found Trump's approval rating holding at 32%, unchanged from the previous week and just one percentage point above the record-low 31% he hit in October.

Republicans also remained behind Democrats on the generic congressional ballot, though the GOP narrowed the gap. Democrats held an eight-percentage-point advantage in the latest poll, down from an 11-point lead the previous week.

Reuters/Ipsos conducted the poll from Oct. 29 to Nov. 2, surveying 1,765 U.S. adults. The poll has a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

Trump delivers closing midterm message at Reflecting Pool

Trump could also be a significant factor in how voters cast their ballots on Nov. 3.

Half of likely voters surveyed by Reuters/Ipsos said their vote would be against Trump, compared with 13% who said they planned to vote in support of the president.

Another 33% said Trump would not be a factor in their vote.

Democrats hold an edge heading into Election Day

Other polling also points to a Democratic advantage in the closing days of the midterm campaign.

An AtlasIntel poll released over the weekend showed Democrats holding a 14-percentage-point lead over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot.

Election forecasts also give Democrats an advantage in the battle for control of Congress. VoteHub gives Democrats an 89% chance of winning the House, projecting 234 seats, and a 68% chance of taking the Senate, with 52 seats projected.

Those forecasts are probabilities rather than predictions of the final results, and control of Congress will ultimately be determined by individual House and Senate races.

Trump's unchanged Reuters/Ipsos rating comes as national polling averages continue to show his approval well underwater.

As of Monday, Nov. 2, the RealClearPolitics average put Trump's approval rating at 39.3%, compared with 58.8% disapproval.

The New York Times polling average showed Trump at 37% approval and 60% disapproval, while Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin average had him at 38.4% approval and 58.8% disapproval.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

articles.title: Maricopa County officials stress Election Day readiness
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Officials in Arizona’s most populous county say they're ready for whatever obstacles arise as roughly a half-million Maricopa County vo...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Officials in Arizona's most populous county say they're ready for whatever obstacles arise as roughly a half-million Maricopa County voters head to the polls on Election Day.

That was stressed during a news conference Monday at the Maricopa County Administration building, where Board of Supervisors Chair Kate Brophy McGee and Deputy Elections Director Jennifer Liewer talked to reporters.

During the Phoenix news conference, Liewer said just over 1,050,000 ballots - or 40% of the county's 2.5 million registered voters - had already been cast, with roughly 950,000 of them being counted, as of Monday.

Liewer said the county expects the quarter-of-a-million Election Day voters to spread out Tuesday across 254 voting locations, up 13.9% from the 223 locations that were in place two years ago.

Liewer projects that there will be roughly the same number of county residents - 250,000, give or take - who will either vote at one of those locations or drop off their early ballots at one.

A new option at county voters' disposal is to take their early ballots to a polling site and have them tabulated right there and then, if they have a valid government-issued ID on them.

While Liewer said the county isn't sure how many voters will choose the new option on Tuesday, she did say that 23,000 people did just that during the Democratic and Republican primaries this summer.

"You can go to any vote center you'd like," Liewer said. "If you work in Glendale, but you live in Mesa, you're able to go vote on your lunch hour in Glendale, and we will print up that ballot that is for you in Mesa with your precincts and your races."

Liewer said the day-of option allows county voters to have added confidence in their electoral system, as they can pick and choose the polling sites that have the shortest wait times on the county's website and get their ballots knocked out quicker.

"Typically, we see our highest numbers after work, so if you have the opportunity to go during the day, you might be able to avoid some of the lines that could happen," she said.

Zach Schira, the assistant county manager, told reporters that the county is expecting to release at 8 p.m. Tuesday the results from all mail-in ballots that were received by Saturday. That's one hour after polls close in the general election.

From there, the county will drop all ballots received through Sunday later in the evening, with results from Monday's final day of early voting and Tuesday's day-of ballots being announced on Wednesday.

Schira said the county has invested in extra elections staff and tabulators to smooth out the process, with 10 to 15% of the ballots being cast or dropped off at a polling site on Tuesday.

"As a reminder, election results are never final on election night," Schira said. "We will have to be counting ballots throughout the week this week, and it is always good to remember that it's the media who calls races, not the county elections department."

Frank McWilliams, director of emergency management security services for the county, said his office is ready to work with law enforcement to ensure a safe experience for all voters come Tuesday.

"We spent the last year planning for this election, and we are ready," McWilliams said. "I'm grateful to all the men and women in law enforcement and all the security personnel for their efforts up to this point, and who will be working on Election Day and the days after, ensuring the safety and security of everyone involved in this election."

McWilliams didn't mince words in response to a question from a Telemundo reporter about what he'd say to those in the Latino community who fear the Trump administration will deploy federal immigration officers to polling stations across the country. McWilliams said officers will ensure everyone can cast their ballots safely.

"Law enforcement will be throughout the community, but it's our goal that voters, poll workers and others don't recognize that we're out and about throughout the community," McWilliams said. "We'll be able to respond appropriately if there's an issue, but we will not have uniformed armed personnel at polling sites visible that may disenfranchise some voters."

articles.summary: James Talarico and Ken Paxton are squaring off for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas. Here's what polls are showing about the race with just one day to go.
articles.body:
Polls show Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead over Republican nominee Ken Paxton in the race for Texas' key Senate seat heading into Election Day.

The race is one of seven battlegrounds that will be crucial to determining partisan control of the Senate in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Talarico leads Paxton by 4 percentage points, according to an average of polling by FiftyPlusOne , a site for political polling and elections.

Here's a look at the recent surveys in the race between Talarico, a member of the Texas House, and Paxton, Texas' attorney general.

Inside President Donald Trump's red state midterm blitz — Photos

Who is leading the Senate race in Texas? See latest polls

Three polls released Nov. 1 showed Talarico leading Paxton.

An AtlasIntel poll showed 51.3% of voters favored Talarico, while 45.4% backed Paxton. The poll, conducted from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1, surveyed more than 1,600 Texas adults with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.2 percentage points.

Another poll, from Siena College and The New York Times , showed 50% of respondents supporting Talarico in the race, while 43% favored Paxton. The poll, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 points, surveyed 1,215 voters and was conducted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1.

Additionally, a YouGov poll shows 51% of those surveyed had or would have voted for Talarico, while 47% had or would vote for Paxton.

An average of polls throughout the race from FiftyPlusOne showed Talarico and Paxton polling evenly until early April, when the Democrat began pulling slightly ahead.
